Speed-to-Power Dominates Energy Costs for AI Data Centers: Technoeconomic Analysis of Powering AI in the Continental United States

Scott Institute for Energy Innovation, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA
Abstract

The rapid growth of artificial intelligence is driving demand for new data centers at large scale and on short deployment timelines. To power them, firms connect to the commercial grid or contract generation directly, but interconnection and gas-turbine delays now incentivize on-site generation. We compare grid-connected and off-grid data center energy infrastructure (AC- and DC-coupled solar-plus-storage, islanded natural gas, and grid interconnection) across the continental U.S. Using an open-source technoeconomic framework built on empirically calibrated AI training loads, climate-driven cooling, stage-by-stage power conversion, and physics-based battery degradation, we model designs providing equivalent energy services. Our central contribution is a speed-adjusted cost of energy that values the compute unlocked by faster construction, making options with different deployment timelines directly comparable on one physically consistent basis. We find DC coupling reduces lifetime energy costs by 18% (9¢/kWh) on average versus AC counterparts by eliminating inverters and improving efficiency. Though rarely cheapest on unadjusted energy cost, DC-coupled microgrids’ faster deployment makes them the lowest-cost modeled option in 85% of U.S. locations once foregone compute is valued, or 55% under accelerated natural gas timelines. For AI infrastructure, deployment speed rather than unit energy cost determines the economically preferred path to power.

1 Introduction

Expanding data center infrastructure to train and deploy cutting-edge artificial intelligence (AI) models is driving a surge in electricity demand in the United States (U.S.) [1, 2]. This breaks a decade of equilibrium: data center energy consumption in the U.S. remained flat in the 2010s as operational efficiency improvements offset growing computational use [3, 4]. The combination of growing AI use, increasing AI model size, and the empirical association between the computational resources allocated to AI models and their performance [5, 6] means operational improvements now fuel expanded capabilities rather than reduced energy consumption.

Specialized hardware performs the computations for AI training and inference in dedicated facilities. Given the performance benefits of high computational density, some of the largest data centers now operate at the scale of hundreds of megawatts of rated power capacity, and announced projects would exceed the energy demand of existing facilities by an order of magnitude [7], on the scale of gigawatts [8]. To avoid falling behind competitors in capabilities and market share, AI infrastructure firms prioritize deployment speed over other considerations [9, 10, 11].

Currently this urgency is confronting a slower physical and policy reality in the legacy electricity system. The utility-planning and regulatory apparatus that reviews interconnection requests, plans capacity, and approves permitting, accustomed to nearly two decades of flat electricity consumption, struggles to meet the growing demands of not only data centers, but the current and future demand from building electrification, vehicle electrification, the growth of major industries, and the other drivers of load growth [12]. Along with these changes, grid interconnection queues (the delay while large loads or new generation await formal approval by local operators to connect to the electric grid and begin construction) are rising, exceeding 5 years in some regions [13, 14, 15, 16, 17]. Beyond administrative capacity, component manufacturing also bottlenecks energy infrastructure: grain-oriented electrical-steel [18], grid transformers [19, 20], high voltage circuit breakers [21], and other electrical transmission and distribution equipment often have multi-year backlogs due to demand outpacing supply. Natural gas combustion turbines for power plants are similarly facing a shortage [22], with new turbine waitlists quoted as ranging from four to seven years across turbine models [23, 24].

In an effort to bypass the slow pace of traditional grid interconnection and begin operations earlier, data centers are using exclusive power purchase agreements (PPA) [25, 26]. Other facilities are developing their own power infrastructure to operate partially [27] or fully islanded from local electric grids [28, 29]. To better understand the physical and economic constraints on the planned expansion of data center infrastructure and associated energy demand, we analyze the technical and economic performance of different off-grid energy solutions for AI data centers across the continental U.S.

AI workloads involve large quantities of parallel operations performed by groups of specialized computer chips, generally termed accelerators, most commonly graphical processing units (GPUs). Accelerators require supervisory CPUs, integrated high-bandwidth memory, and high-performance networking and interconnection components. This bundle of hardware is referred to as a compute node. Nodes are analogous to a traditional enterprise server, though they draw 10-20 times the power, with a group of nodes referred to as a cluster, an 8-GPU configuration being a current commercial standard [30].

AI model development involves two phases: training, during which models learn from massive datasets through intense computation; and inference, when trained models process queries to generate output. While both training and inference involve periods of high computational intensity, training workloads are especially challenging to energy systems. Large-scale training for frontier models can require months of continuous operation, with individual nodes demanding 70-80% on average of their manufacturer rated maximum power for the duration of the training [1, 31, 32].

Electricity demand “in-workload” during training is flat at hourly or daily granularity, but locally, the power demand of individual nodes can fluctuate by thousands of watts in periods of just milliseconds [33, 32], with fluctuations time correlated across all involved nodes. Transients at these frequencies on cluster scale strain electric grids [34] that serve commercial AI data centers [35, 36] and high-performance scientific computing facilities [37, 38]. This can reduce local power quality, both within the data center, disrupting other compute nodes, and beyond it, affecting sensitive electrical loads (such as hospitals and other data centers) as well as nearby residential utility customers. While infrastructure upgrades can address these transients, the cost allocation mechanism used to assure a minimum level of power quality can have broader impacts. Within our analysis, we bound the facility-level cost of managing these transients (Results, Robustness and Sensitivity Analysis).

Electrical utilities charge customers both a capacity fee and a per-kilowatt-hour fee to recover generation costs and fixed transmission and distribution infrastructure costs. Even when there is sufficient existing generation capacity to meet data center loads [39, 12], new data centers can drive up local electricity prices as ratepayers finance infrastructure upgrades to transmit and distribute power. A recent report by the Virginia legislature found typical residential customers could face $37 per month higher electricity costs due to data center infrastructure expansion [40], and a national projection of electricity cost found increases by up to 57% in some regions by 2030 [41].

Data center electricity consumption consists of IT equipment (servers, storage, networking) plus cooling and power distribution infrastructure. Cooling costs vary dramatically by climate: cold regions achieve near-optimal performance through free cooling, while hot, humid locations require energy-intensive mechanical chillers [42]. Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE), the dimensionless ratio of total facility power to IT power, quantifies this overhead, with the highest performing facilities approaching the theoretical performance limit of 1.0.

Operational electricity generally comprises over 90% of a data center’s environmental footprint [43, 44], with carbon intensity, water use [45], and cost varying substantially by location. The performance of wind, solar, and geothermal assets varies according to local conditions. This spatial heterogeneity means no single microgrid architecture is likely to be best across all locations.

Previous work by Baranko et al. [46] examined both the geographic and speed-to-deployment performance of solar and storage microgrids for AI data centers. The authors noted that while clean-firm generating technologies such as small-modular nuclear or advanced geothermal show promise for data center applications, their deployment supply chains are unlikely to mature in time to meet near-term AI demand. They found that the geographic potential for solar based microgrids in the United States was substantial [47] and that the estimated two-year combined permitting and construction timeline presented a key advantage for these technologies.

The performance of solar and battery-energy-storage system (BESS) microgrids also varies according to system architecture: the generation and storage technology together with the AC or DC power-distribution scheme. Unlike thermal, hydroelectric, and wind power plants, solar photovoltaic (PV) panels generate direct current (DC) electricity. Because the U.S. power grid operates at 60 Hz alternating current (AC), connecting PV systems to the grid requires an inverter, a power-electronic device that converts this DC output into the 3-phase, 60 Hz AC and a power transformer to match grid voltage. Any voltage or current conversion step necessarily introduces some operational losses. Dispatchable storage resources like BESS and reversible fuel cells are notably charged by and discharge DC. To avoid conversion and clipping losses, storage and PV systems can interface prior to inversion, a microgrid architecture known as DC coupled. DC coupling improves system cost [48, 49], efficiency [50, 51], and reliability [52, 53].

While data centers typically require power at a variety of different voltage levels, they are unusually well suited to accommodate DC power distribution. An idealized data center contains only IT and cooling loads: chips already operate on DC power, with power supply (PSU) or power distribution (PDU) units typically performing the necessary voltage conversions. The primary electrical load for cooling is the motor powering fans, pumps, and compressors. Motor drives or electronic speed controllers perform the necessary voltage conversions, and are highly efficient. Although most often these are AC induction motors, the improvement in brushless DC motors shows potential for a fully DC facility. Further, electricity use is the primary operating cost of a data center, meaning the economic case for efficient DC power systems infrastructure in data centers is stronger than in most other facilities [54, 55, 56]. For these reasons, previous research has explored all-DC data center designs [57, 58], with pilot facilities in the United States [59], Japan [60], and Europe [61].

There are gaps and limitations within this literature. Previous microgrid modeling for AI data centers has relied on static assumptions for cooling, power systems losses, or the off-grid natural gas case. Although separate research communities have investigated the advantages of DC power architectures for both solar+storage systems and data centers independently, to date, no work has explored the efficiency gains from integrating these approaches. While industry emphasis on deployment speed is well documented, no open framework exists for quantifying the tradeoffs between speed and cost. Each of these unknown quantities is decision-relevant and can potentially shift which architecture a developer should select.

In this work we develop an open-source, end-to-end technoeconomic model of self-supplied power for AI data centers (Fig. 1). For a given scale and location, we construct an hourly facility load—empirically calibrated, near-baseload AI training demand plus weather-driven cooling performance. We design and dispatch three islanded architectures, AC and DC solar-plus-storage and islanded natural gas with diesel backup, comparing them against grid interconnection. Because each architecture must deliver equivalent energy service at equivalent reliability, and every shared input is held identical across cases, the resulting cost differences are attributable to the architectures themselves rather than to differences in assumptions between them. We evaluate each option on two axes: levelized cost of energy, and the time value of energized compute. We find that scale and location shift gas competitiveness enough to redraw the map of preferred architectures, and that DC coupling materially lowers lifetime energy cost relative to AC distribution. Quantifying the value of deployment speed through the time value of energized compute, we find that it dominates differences in unit energy cost in selecting the preferred architecture. The speed-premium concept generalizes to other time-sensitive capital-deployment decisions beyond data centers.

2 Methods

Our analysis proceeds in three stages. First, we develop the hourly facility load that any power system must serve, combining IT demand with location-specific cooling requirements. Second, we simulate candidate power distribution systems meeting this load profile, tracking hourly energy flows from generation through storage and conversion to final consumption. Third, we search each architecture’s design space (varying design parameters such as battery capacity or turbine model within allowable configurations) to identify configurations that minimize levelized cost while achieving required reliability. Comprehensively detailed methods and a full inventory of modeling parameters are available in the Supplementary Information.

We compare four power architectures (AC solar+storage, DC solar+storage, islanded natural gas with diesel backup, grid interconnection) serving equivalent IT and cooling loads at a particular location with identical reliability requirements. While cooling performance differs by locations, and power systems vary how efficiently they deliver energy from source to load, in a given location, for a given quantity of GPUs, all architectures must deliver equivalent energy services at equivalent reliability.

We model AI training specialized facilities, operating at near baseload utilization [62], composed of a fleet of identical 8-H100 node equivalents: avg power 7.3 kW, max 8.5 kW inclusive of memory and interconnect components [33]. We calculate hourly PUE using Lei and Masanet’s framework [42], selecting the minimum annual PUE option for the location. Power systems are configured sufficient to deliver the maximum IT load multiplied by the 99th percentile PUE and a 1.05 contingency factor. We index facility scale by GPU count and report the corresponding peak as a design load in megawatts (a 100,000-GPU facility, for example, has a design load of roughly 131 MW); average draw is lower, but power infrastructure is scoped to this peak. We compare each system in simulation year 27, end-of-life for the PV modules (25 year lifespan), with a base-case discount rate of 7%. For scenarios with BESS, we assume one single end-of-life replacement of the battery modules occurring at the conclusion of operational year 13. All financial values are in 2022 dollars, and all discounting occurs mid-year.

To compare different microgrid systems, we develop candidate power-flow models of all paths between generation and facility loads, with the associated conversion losses. We model all power systems outward from the main low-voltage distribution bus, accumulating the efficiency of every voltage and conversion step to each load and from each source. The candidate power system architectures are shown in Figure 2, and more comprehensive discussion of their design and efficiency is available in the Supplementary Information. Grid-connected and natural-gas facilities follow conventional AC data-center architecture [63, 64, 65], with the natural-gas generator terminal voltage (13-19 kV depending on turbine) stepped up to a facility medium-voltage distribution spine (34.5 kV) and then stepped down to 480 V AC in the data hall.

Our PV+storage microgrids are based on typical centralized generation and storage designs, with panel collection strings wired into 1500 V DC blocks. We consider two distribution architectures: a small, modular layout with a single low-voltage bus serving co-located generation, storage, and load; and a medium-voltage layout in which an MV spine separates centralized generation from the data-hall loads and distributes power across the campus, as ampacity and PV gathering constraints require at scale. The medium-voltage topologies are the primary cases; we detail the LV architectures in the Supplementary Information (Supplementary Network Topology and Storage Placement; Supplementary Fig. 12). In the low-voltage AC case, storage is coupled to the data-hall switchgear through grid-forming inverters. In the medium-voltage case, power from the grid-forming inverters passes through a step-up transformer to the 34.5 kV AC distribution spine, then steps down to 480 V AC (3-phase) at the data hall.

In the AC architecture, the bulk of storage is DC-coupled to the PV field, sharing the PV inverter and charging upstream of it. In the all-DC architecture, it is instead centralized off the ±10 kV spine [66]. In both, a smaller increment of approximately the nameplate power of the load it protects (on the order of 2 MW of combined load and storage per LV spur [67, 68, 69]) is distributed to the data-hall LV buses for local outage protection, and in the AC case for grid-forming. Provisioning this distributed increment changes LCOE by 1% or less compared to the purely centralized case. In the primary AC case, we assume these local grid-forming pods maintain power quality through training transients without full double-conversion isolation IT power. See the Supplementary Network Topology and Storage Placement section for more detailed discussion, including the cost performance of different topologies and headline cost of instead double-conversion conditioning the full load.

In the medium voltage all-DC microgrids, the 1500 V DC blocks are stepped up to ±\pm10 kV for distribution across the campus [70, 71, 72, 73], and then stepped down to low distribution voltage within the data hall. Note that within the data hall (∼\sim30 MW), loads are containerized into ∼\sim2MW [74, 69, 72] low-voltage blocks to limit both continuous bus currents and prospective fault currents to within the interrupting capability of available DC protection. Within the data hall, the embedded battery’s DC/DC charge controller handles grid-forming through droop-voltage regulation, distributing power on a ±\pm400V bus [75]. Server power supplies and cooling motor drives perform the final conversion to load voltage. This design is compliant with the emerging OCP standard [76]. We obtained our design logic, component efficiencies, and performance data from component datasheets, operational estimates from industry experts, existing all-DC pilots, and efficiency curve data [77, 78, 59, 79, 53, 48, 67, 72, 80].

To simulate PV+BESS microgrid systems, we adopt the vectorized hourly energy balance approach from [81, 46], modified with a bus-centric architecture that explicitly models conversion losses through different power-flow paths. The PV generation model fetches TMY weather data (irradiance and temperature) for the specified coordinates from the National Solar Resource Database (NSRDB) [82] and feeds these into pvlib’s ModelChain to calculate DC power output. We assume the battery system is composed of the underlying modules in 4-hour, 60 MW Lithium-Iron-Phosphate (LFP) packs, each rated to store a total of 240 MWh of usable energy [83], though note that this system is comprised of 48 containerized 1.25 MW units. We chose these battery modules because they are well characterized in the literature and represent the current commercial standard. Note that minimum capacity increment for commercial designs is on the order of 1 MW of rated capacity, and we discuss sensitivity to step size and cost sensitivity of explicit incremental modeling as opposed to continuous optimization in the Supplementary Information.

We select LFP as our battery chemistry due to its excellent durability and ramp rate [84] and current commercial deployment in grid-scale storage applications. The hourly dispatch algorithm prioritizes serving facility load from solar generation. Surplus solar charges the battery (subject to power rating and available headroom), with remainder curtailed. Deficits trigger battery discharge (subject to power rating and stored energy). Supplementary Fig. 1 traces this dispatch over a representative week. Component degradation follows established empirical models: solar modules degrade linearly (1% first year from light-induced degradation, then 0.55% annually) [85]. Batteries follow BLAST-Lite’s [86] empirically calibrated physics-based framework for LFP calendar aging and cycling stress as functions of temperature, state-of-charge, and charge-discharge patterns. We model mid-life battery replacement at year 13, reflecting industry practice of discrete infrastructure upgrades rather than continuous capacity additions. See Supplementary Methods for more details, with Supplementary Figs. 2-4 characterizing battery fade dynamics and the performance of our computational proxy, Supplementary Fig. 9 illustrating optimization stability and the Supplementary Sensitivity Analysis section discussing alternative battery replacement timing and augmentation strategy.

Natural gas combustion turbine power plant design differs from PV system optimization due to its discrete solution space: multiple interacting discontinuities that preclude simple scaling from reference designs. We generate candidate plant configurations using a library of commercially available turbines, apply engineering constraints derived from industry practice, and evaluate the full lifecycle economics of each specific configuration. Our design tool proceeds from a library of 16 reference natural gas turbine models classified as aeroderivative, F-class, or H-class. We model turbine performance accounting for part-load efficiency penalties, ambient temperature derating, and combined-cycle plant configurations where applicable. We adopt a configuration specific auxiliary load [87] empirically calibrated to EIA reference plant values [88]. We filter designs to those capable of delivering minimum facility power as defined in the facility load, operating within code-compliant load factor bounds, and passing design filters to reflect operational plant configurations (no mixed model fleets, etc.) We scope backup diesel systems to supply minimum facility power, and model annual diesel operations as matching the gas plant’s expected annual unserved energy from planned maintenance and forced outages. We evaluate lifecycle costs for all filtered configurations and select the minimum-cost option. See Supplementary Methods for implementation details.

We calculate LCOE for each candidate design as the ratio of the sum of the present value of costs to the sum of the present value of delivered energy. We source PV+storage capital costs from NLR’s Annual Technology Baseline (ATB) [88], disaggregated into component-level costs using detailed breakdowns from [89], with land requirements parameterized at 4.17 acres-per-MW DC [90, 91]. Operating costs for PV came from [89] and battery storage O&M from the PNNL energy storage cost database [92]. Natural gas plant costs are from NLR ATB [88] for F-class and H-class turbines and EIA’s Annual Energy Outlook [93] for aeroderivatives, with costs scaled to specific capacities using empirical scaling exponents of 0.67 for capital and 0.80 for fixed O&M following established engineering practice [94, 95]. For a data center in a location, an optimization algorithm searches through the uptime-compliant designs within each architecture for the LCOE minimizing configuration.

We model project development timelines based on industry data and expert consultation. Solar+storage systems follow a 24-month timeline consistent with [46] and validated by industry experts. Natural gas plants use construction estimates from [93]: 40 months for simple cycle and 42 months for combined cycle configurations, with turbine delivery (conservatively estimated at 36 months based on fastest reported timeline by OEM) as the potential rate-limiting factor. We assume 30% of construction is bottlenecked by turbine delivery; remaining work proceeds in parallel. For grid interconnection, we use supply-side queue data from [13] as a proxy, assigning each state the 2018-2023 median duration from initial request to commercial operation for its ISO/RTO region. See the Supplementary Information for implementation detail.

Data centers contain GPUs that could generate revenue immediately if deployed elsewhere. Each month of construction represents foregone computational output: training runs not completed, models not deployed, competitive position ceded to faster rivals. This opportunity cost varies dramatically between architectures: grid interconnection requiring 5 years represents 3 years of lost operations compared to 2-year solar construction.

We quantify opportunity cost using GPU spot market rental rates. At $2.40/GPU-hour (H100 rental index price in y0y_{0} dollars [96]), an operator unable to extract at least this value should rationally rent their compute to the market. This rental price thus represents the floor utility of the marginal GPU-hour committed to an internal workload. For hyperscalers balancing frontier model training (likely worth substantially more) against routine inference and fine-tuning (potentially worth less), this spot price provides a reasonable value proxy. For AI-specialized firms running exclusively proprietary training workloads, it likely understates value.

We calculate the value of lost compute in year tt, V​L​CtVLC_{t}, as the idle GPU-hours multiplied by rental rate for all pre-operational years (Eq. 1):

VLCt=∑h=0Hidle,tNGPU×pspot\text{VLC}_{t}=\sum_{h=0}^{H_{\text{idle},t}}N_{\text{GPU}}\times p_{\text{spot}} (1)

We incorporate foregone compute value as an opportunity cost during construction years of any given system, creating a speed-adjusted LCOE that endogenizes deployment timeline (Eq. 2):

LCOEadj=∑t=0n(Ccap,t+Cop,t+VLCt)(1+r)t+0.5∑t=0nEt(1+r)t+0.5\text{LCOE}_{\text{adj}}=\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{(C_{\text{cap},t}+C_{\text{op},t}+\text{VLC}_{t})}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}}{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{E_{t}}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}} (2)

where nn is the evaluation year common across analyzed scenarios.

We test sensitivity across GPU valuations from $1.00-4.00/hr and construction timeline variations of ±\pm50% to assess how these parameters affect architectural selection (see Results and the Supplementary Information).

3 Results

Here we outline how our modeled energy system performance varies both by location and by microgrid architecture. Unless otherwise stated, figures depict systems scoped for 99% annual availability—that is, the islanded microgrid satisfies the facility’s full IT-and-cooling load in at least 99% of hours over the year (equivalently, 99% GPU uptime), with the small remainder treated as unserved.

3.1 Architectural Comparison

We find that all-DC architectures outperform equivalent AC systems on cost, with an average all-DC advantage of almost 9 cents per kWh (18%), consistent with the energy performance observed in a pilot [97]. At scale this returns material savings. Consider a 100,000-GPU, ∼\sim131 MW design-load facility in the Permian Basin of West Texas. The all-DC microgrid delivers energy at $0.27/kWh against $0.33/kWh for the otherwise-identical AC system, a saving of $0.062/kWh. Because both are PV+BESS systems, this gap is avoided hardware: eliminated inverters and higher path efficiency that let the all-DC system meet the same load with less installed generation and storage. This represents a $570 million reduction in the net present value of energy costs. For systems of this scale, even minor improvements in efficiency return significant absolute savings.

DC cost advantages are not uniform across the U.S., as shown in Figure 3. Locations differ in the fraction of annual energy that flows directly from PV-to-load versus through the BESS-charge-discharge-load pathway. MV DC power distribution improves efficiency along both battery discharge and PV to load pathways, but it achieves largest performance gains on the battery discharge pathway and by avoiding inverters. See Supplementary Network Topology and Storage Placement for more detailed discussion of the cost drivers of different topologies.

Across the continental United States, levelized cost varies within each PV architecture by roughly $0.40/kWh over the central range of locations (5th–95th percentile) and double that spread between the cheapest and most expensive sites. This variation is set less by a location’s average solar resource (a long-run climate feature) than by the depth of its worst sustained low-solar stretch (a within-year weather extreme). The system must ride through the longest cloudy spell, and system LCOE tracks the worst five-day insolation window far more closely than annual insolation. Two sites can receive essentially identical annual sunlight yet differ severalfold in cost. At roughly 5​kWh/m2/day5~\mathrm{kWh/m^{2}/day} of insolation, a dry interior-West Colorado site and a fog-prone northern-California site differ nearly threefold in cost ($0.21 vs. $0.61/kWh), because the latter’s worst five-day power production window is dramatically worse.

While medium voltage PV-based microgrids are predictably sensitive to local geographic conditions, they are insensitive to facility scale. Modularity penalties remain negligible (<0.3%<0.3\% median) across realistic component sizes and decrease with system scale; see Supplementary Methods for more detail. When considering the low voltage architectures, either for a small facility, or modular designs comprised of multiple containers, costs decrease a median 2.4% for DC and 3.7% for AC compared to their respective medium-voltage counterparts. In contrast, natural gas plants display significant scale economies, as shown in Figure 4: costs decline sharply as facility capacity increases. Small aeroderivative plants operating at 10-20 MW achieve LCOEs of $0.25-0.30/kWh, while large combined-cycle configurations decline towards marginal grid prices. The discontinuous structure in these cost curves reflects discrete turbine unit additions and transitions between designs as optimal configurations shift.

Regional variation in fuel costs and solar resources significantly affects system costs. In the Colorado location shown in Figure 4, natural gas plants achieve cost parity with DC-coupled microgrids around 30 MW facility capacity. Elevated gas prices would shift this crossover point toward larger facilities, and cheaper gas or lower solar productivity locations shift the crossover towards smaller facilities. Natural gas prices and DC microgrid costs (see Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6) vary by more than a factor of three across U.S. locations, creating substantially different economic landscapes for off-grid AI data centers.

Our fully-islanded cases model operation entirely off-grid, but facilities might opt for a hybrid system. Such facilities would operate for some fraction of the year on islanded power, and would otherwise be grid supplied. Figure 5 shows the performance of microgrids of different architecture as we vary their expected annual usage. Solar-based microgrids require a disproportionate share of investment to increase reliability: each additional “nine” of availability—90% (one nine), 99% (two nines), 99.9% (three nines)-requires more capacity. This mirrors macro electricity systems, where infrastructure must be scoped for the worst-case scenario. In the natural gas case, this contingency scoping is effectively priced-in to building a facility capable of delivering baseload power; higher utilization more effectively economizes that upfront investment.

LCOE varies by architecture, facility scale, and geography. Natural gas systems are more cost-effective for large scales across most locations. DC-coupled microgrids are cost-competitive for smaller facilities, and in regions with high-insolation, particularly the solar alley spanning southern California, Arizona, Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico as shown in Supplementary Figs. 5 and 6. This reflects fundamentally different cost structures: natural gas systems spread fixed costs more favorably across greater energy output, while both MV and LV PV+BESS costs scale near-linearly with capacity. Notably, when considering only unadjusted LCOE, microgrids of all architectures are generally dominated by grid interconnection, though our grid costs represent a lower bound (see discussion for details).

3.2 Speed-to-Power Premium

Incorporating a premium for the speed of deployment alters the architectural comparison results: DC-coupled microgrids prove lowest-cost among our modeled options across 84.9% of the U.S. Grid interconnection out-competes where cheap electricity and fast interconnection align, as shown in Figure 6A. Deployment speed dominates other considerations as the value of lost compute (V​L​CVLC) ultimately proves more consequential than unadjusted LCOE (Methods, Eqs. 1–2). This V​L​CVLC framework applies equally to operational reliability targets. Moving from 90% to 99% uptime is worth approximately $0.20/kWh in avoided lost computing value, while the incremental value of each additional nine falls by roughly an order of magnitude. When we evaluate DC-coupled solar systems across each DOE climate zone, the marginal cost of moving from one to two nines falls below this threshold in all but one case (Seattle, WA), but no location justifies the incremental cost of moving to very high availability (+99.9%) on compute value alone.

A DC solar system’s deployment speed advantage makes it the default choice across most locations, but where solar resources are sufficiently poor, an opening emerges for alternatives that outcompete on unit energy costs. Grid competitiveness depends on whether the combination of electricity prices and interconnection timelines can overcome the speed disadvantage.

For example, Maine and upstate New York illustrate this dynamic: both regions feature among the worst solar resources in the U.S. The grid is the lowest L​C​O​Ea​d​jLCOE_{adj} architecture in Maine despite moderate electricity prices due to the nation’s fastest interconnection timeline. NYISO’s longer interconnection queue makes DC solar preferable despite moderate utility rates and unimpressive PV performance.

In regions with adequate-to-good solar resources, grid connection succeeds only where inexpensive industrial electricity combines with short interconnection timelines. East Texas and Georgia exemplify this pathway: each has industrial electricity rates below 6¢ / kWh paired with three-year interconnection, making grid connection the lowest L​C​O​EadjLCOE_{\text{adj}} modeled option in these locations.

Natural gas combustion turbine systems are disadvantaged when considering V​L​CVLC due to correlated regional factors that eliminate the competitive niche. Local gas prices and grid electricity costs correlate because gas-fired generation sets marginal wholesale prices in most markets. Consequently, locations favorable for gas microgrids on engineering costs, such as East Texas, likely also feature inexpensive grid power. There are few locations where gas prices are low enough, interconnection queues long enough, and solar expensive enough that gas is preferred under our baseline assumptions.

To assess robustness of this finding, we parametrically vary the two main determinants of V​L​CVLC: interconnection speed and the value of a chip-hour. Figure 7 shows the internal value of a GPU-hour at which a firm would be indifferent between an all-DC microgrid and grid interconnection under baseline interconnection timelines. This threshold varies geographically from <$1.00<\$1.00/hr in high-insolation regions to >$4.00>\$4.00/hr in solar-poor locations (median indifference value: $1.61 / chip-hour), indicating that architectural choice depends critically on both firm-specific valuations and location-specific resources. See Supplementary Fig. 7 for an analogous plot for the indifference interconnection speed holding V​L​CVLC fixed.

We also consider an accelerated natural gas deployment case, in which gas combustion turbine microgrids are operational after only three years. This would reflect either idealized plant construction parallelization or significantly ahead-of-schedule turbine delivery. Figure 6B shows how the minimum L​C​O​EadjLCOE_{\text{adj}} for a 100,000 GPU facility changes under this accelerated natural gas timeline. DC solar remains the minimum cost modeled architecture in 55.6% of U.S. locations. Natural gas microgrids rise to be the lowest L​C​O​EadjLCOE_{\text{adj}} of the modeled options in 35.2% of locations, showing clear regional deployment patterns: the solar-poor and grid-sluggish areas of the Midwest, the Appalachian Basin, and Cascadia. Grid interconnection remains the L​C​O​EadjLCOE_{\text{adj}} preferred option in 9.2% of analyzed locations: New England, East Texas, and the interior Southeast. Even under an optimistic natural gas construction timeline, DC solar retains majority deployment preference, and grid interconnection remains preferred in specific regions (New England, East Texas). See Supplementary Fig. 8 for a plot of the indifference natural gas plant construction speed.

3.3 Robustness and Sensitivity Analysis

We evaluate how parameter uncertainty affects both system costs and architectural selection through two complementary approaches: varying inputs for fixed designs to bound cost uncertainty, and re-optimizing under modified inputs and modeling assumptions to test robustness. We present our summary findings of this analysis below, see the Supplementary Sensitivity Analysis section for more comprehensive discussion.

For fixed designs, natural gas costs are dominated by fuel price: the continental-U.S. range (Oklahoma to California) creates $0.08–0.11/kWh spreads that exceed the impact of discount-rate or capital-cost uncertainty. Solar+storage costs respond most strongly to the discount rate (a 27–43% variation across 3–12% rates); balance-of-system and battery costs have second-order impacts, and land cost is negligible—requiring a sixfold increase to match even battery O&M, the next lowest cost influence parameter.

To gauge the robustness of the per-location architecture choice, we flag each tile in which a second architecture falls within a 1¢/kWh envelope of the lowest-LCOEadj\text{LCOE}_{\text{adj}} option. Under baseline assumptions, 149 of 4,317 locations (3.5%) sit in this near-indifferent band, all at the solar–grid boundary; under the accelerated three-year gas case the count rises to 348 (8.1%), the additional count split roughly evenly between DC-solar (168 tiles) and gas-preferring (136 tiles) locations, with the remainder grid. These near-indifferent tiles remain a small minority and do not skew toward any one technology as runner-up.

Re-optimization leaves both the selected design and its cost stable. Across the plausible range of each technical performance input the re-optimized cost moves little: battery round-trip efficiency is the largest single lever, at −2.6%-2.6\% to +3.2%+3.2\% over 0.85–0.95, and power-conversion component efficiencies shift cost by ±\pm1–3%. The selected design itself rarely changes: of 72 natural gas parameter variations across four scales, only five altered the chosen turbine configuration, each a power-electronics improvement that let a smaller plant clear the minimum-load filter. Across independent optimizer seeds, the recovered designs agree within ∼\sim1% in LCOE (median over fourteen sites), while component size varies more (5–7%), indicating a near-flat cost basin in which solar and battery capacity substitute on the margin (see Supplementary Information Optimization Stability for more detail).

Two modeling choices warrant focused treatment. First, in the base case, we replace the battery once, at year 13. Re-anchoring the degradation schedule to a year-10 or year-16 replacement and re-optimizing shifts LCOE by −0.6%-0.6\% to +5.1%+5.1\% (AC) and −1.1%-1.1\% to +3.5%+3.5\% (DC), and moves the optimal battery capacity itself by a few percent, as later replacement requires somewhat more initial storage to hold reliability through the more-degraded pre-replacement year. Replacing only faded capacity through fixed-period augmentation (installing additional modules to replace faded capacity but keeping the existing fleet in use), rather than swapping the full system, reduces LCOE by roughly 8%. These results are consistent with the high state-of-health (≈\approx89%) of the modules in the modeled replacement year. We retain full replacement in our baseline case as a deliberately conservative operational assumption.

Second, we size each system against a single typical meteorological year (TMY). Re-optimized against each historical year from 2010 to 2023 at 28 sites spanning all 14 DOE climate zones, TMY proves a mildly optimistic design: it sits a median 4.5% ($0.012/kWh) below the historical-year mean (Supplementary Fig. 11). This is a right-skewed tail effect, not a uniform offset: the reliability constraint makes cost a nonlinear function of the worst sustained multi-day cloudy stretch. Stitching together a composite of broadly typical months necessarily tends to trim the worst-in-a-decade stretches. As an estimator of the across-year mean cost, TMY is nonetheless about twice as precise as a single randomly drawn year (See Supplementary Information Design-year weather sensitivity for more detail).

Fuel-price volatility enters only the natural gas case, and its magnitude is fixed at design time. Smaller facilities are limited to fuel-exposed simple-cycle plants (a committed elasticity near 0.0116 $/kWh per $/MMBtu, nearly independent of location); only sufficiently large facilities (≳\gtrsim180 MW, in high-fuel-price regions) adopt the lower-heat-rate combined cycle (Supplementary Fig. 10). A large facility that is averse to fuel-price risk, or expects prices to rise, can therefore choose combined-cycle configuration partly as a fuel price hedge, exchanging higher capital cost for a more favorable heat rate. This option is not economically available to small turbine plants. Propagating each state’s historical price dispersion through the committed plant moves LCOE within a 5th–95th-percentile band of roughly $0.005–0.024/kWh (median ∼\sim$0.011/kWh) with no shift in the central estimate.

Choices internal to the power system change the results less than the architecture itself. Reallocating storage among the PV field, the medium-voltage spine, and the data hall changes LCOE within ±\pm1.5%. The one exception is power conditioning: routing the entire IT load through online double-conversion, rather than maintaining quality through grid-forming alone, adds ∼\sim5.9% to base LCOE (∼\sim6.4% when also conditioning cooling). These values reflect our modeled topologies under full conditioning; how much of the load a facility must condition, and how aggressively, varies with hardware [34], load profile, and the tolerance of co-located loads. The all-DC advantage itself decomposes into a cumulative-distribution-path-efficiency component of ∼\sim7.9% and a roughly equivalent avoided-capital component from the eliminated inverter and AC collection equipment. This delta persists unless DC-side balance-of-system costs approach double our central estimate (see Supplementary Information Sensitivity Analysis).

4 Discussion

For planned AI data centers in the continental U.S., we find the value of deployment speed overwhelms differences in energy costs. This result highlights an economic advantage for solar+storage microgrids, which can operate after 24-month construction timelines. Conversely, grid interconnection can take 4-5 years, creating substantial opportunity costs in lost computing revenue as a result of the delay in beginning operations. Islanded microgrids avoid interconnection studies and associated regulatory delays, though quantifying geographic variation in permitting timelines remains beyond this analysis. Under optimistic natural gas combustion turbine deployment scenarios (36 months), DC-coupled solar remains lowest-cost among our modeled options in 55% of continental U.S. locations.

4.1 Limitations

We adopt several simplifying assumptions that could affect our results. Most consequentially, we model grid interconnection as purchasing industrial electricity at prevailing rates after an interconnection delay [98]. This omits the cost of infrastructure upgrades that large loads may trigger: substation expansion, transformer procurement, transmission reinforcement, and reconductoring. While utilities nominally bear these costs, they recover them through rates, effectively creating cross-subsidies to data centers from other ratepayers. Accurately modeling such infrastructure costs would increase the grid LCOE by an uncertain but potentially substantial amount. Our comparison therefore represents a lower bound on grid costs, strengthening our finding that microgrids are competitive even in the face of optimistically modeled grid scenarios.

We estimate grid interconnection timelines from the regional median duration of the supply-side queue from [13], assigned at the ISO/RTO or state level. This proxy has known limitations: demand-side interconnection processes may differ systematically from supply-side requests, and state-level aggregation obscures any intrastate variation in queue congestion. Supply-side queues represent the best-available empirical benchmarks for large-load interconnection timelines.

We design systems using typical meteorological year (TMY) data, but industry-leading uptime will require systems to survive worst-case, not average years. Re-optimizing against each historical year from 2010–2023 confirms TMY to be a mildly optimistic sizing basis, a median 4.5% ($0.012/kWh) below the historical-year mean. Our hourly simulation therefore captures average conditions well but may modestly undersize solar+BESS systems relative to what firms would deploy to manage weather extremes. Additionally, our use of single-location TMY datasets means adjacent locations with similar long-term climates may show diverging results if their TMY datasets captured different realizations of weather, particularly in regions with high spatial climate heterogeneity.

We assume mature supply chains for DC power systems that in some cases do not yet exist at scale. Design standards remain uncodified, some DC fault protection equipment is precommercial, and the skilled workforce overwhelmingly specializes in AC systems. Power electronics datasheets provide our component values, but integrated system performance at 100+ MW requires empirical validation. The 9¢/kWh average DC advantage represents expected savings; early deployments may capture only partial gains while encountering integration challenges and supply chain constraints we do not model. Trade or geopolitical disruptions to the supply of PV modules or LFP cathodes would delay deployment.

Our natural gas modeling uses state-level industrial gas prices as uniform proxies, obscuring intrastate heterogeneity. Facilities near pipeline hubs may face lower costs than modeled, while remote locations could face premiums. The natural gas turbines we modeled span aeroderivative, F-class, and H-class units, with representative performance. However this does not exhaustively catalog all generator models, primarily affecting discrete optimization space rather than fundamental cost trends.

Our central estimates treat fuel and grid electricity prices as fixed regional averages. We bound the effect of natural-gas fuel-price volatility in a sensitivity analysis (Results, Robustness and Sensitivity Analysis), finding it modest, but we do not model grid electricity price fluctuations, nor do we carry these risk premia through into our central LCOE. Solar+storage microgrids offer the strongest cost certainty: after initial capital recovery, operational costs are predictable, and more importantly, very low. In contrast, natural gas systems face commodity price risk throughout their operational life, though long-term supply contracts can partially hedge this exposure. Grid-connected facilities face both fuel price passthrough and regulatory uncertainty in rate structures. These omitted certainty premia likely favor solar microgrids on average, as they eliminate exposure to both fuel and regulatory risk, while potentially improving gas systems’ relative attractiveness over grid connection in markets where capacity contracts lock in fuel costs but retail electricity prices remain volatile.

Our analysis assumes frictionless land acquisition for all generating technologies. Solar installations at modeled scales require hundreds to thousands of acres, while natural gas facilities require substantially smaller operational footprints. However, all energy infrastructure faces siting challenges including environmental assessments, zoning approvals, and community opposition. Our sensitivity analysis shows land costs themselves have negligible impact on LCOE. If acquisition challenges manifest primarily as higher costs rather than timeline delays, this limitation has minimal effect on our findings. However, if land acquisition significantly extends deployment timelines asymmetrically across technologies, it could alter the speed premium dynamics that drive our comparative findings.

4.2 Future Work

Future work should empirically assess the performance of the DC power systems for AI data centers. DC facilities use bus voltage as their primary control signal, and the ability to maintain that voltage under transients depends on the slew rate and response time of the individual components. If the BESS lack sufficient ramping capabilities, or if the duty-cycle would dramatically alter the system stressor, facilities might require additional components for fast droop voltage control (e.g. supercapacitors). Converter or microgrid-energy-management-system performance may also represent a bottleneck. Notably, LFP cells are capable of rapid ramping [99], and routinely interface with PV installations that exhibit comparable transients [100], meaning LFP batteries show technical promise as the regulator of bus voltage in these systems.

Modeling heterogeneous compute fleets and varied workloads (e.g., training and inference, different node types) would require only minor modifications. This would enable analysis of more complex facility operations, including fleet dispatching and distributed computing. While not all workloads are amenable to this kind of distribution and demand response (memory throughput and interconnect latency can make this infeasible in training, and some inference is time sensitive), both distributed training [101] and the scheduling optimization [102, 103] are ongoing areas of research. Future work could expand to model facilities serving more diverse workloads, and compare the energy systems costs of concentrating or distributing those computational capabilities between single or multiple facilities.

Future research should analyze microgrids based on other technologies, including nuclear (both conventional light-water reactors and emerging advanced nuclear designs), advanced geothermal, wind, reciprocating engine, and mixed portfolios. Wind resources are a fuel-free option plentiful in the solar-poor region of the upper Midwest [104]. Mixed architectures could leverage the complementarities between wind and solar generation [105], and natural gas fuel cells could solve the "last mile" of reliability for an otherwise PV and battery-based all DC system. This framework could identify the deployment speed at which these emerging generation technologies can economically compete with mature generation-and-storage systems.

4.3 Implications

AI training workloads align well with solar+storage technical characteristics. AI training runs last months with significant post-processing, enabling facility siting in high-insolation regions without performance penalties. High-reliability microgrid requirements (99%+ uptime) necessitate substantial battery capacity, but the resulting steady daily discharge pattern creates benign duty cycles that maintain storage lifespans beyond modeled replacement intervals.

Beyond energy supply, battery storage enables proactive facility management. Storage provides hours of response time to address potential supply shortfalls, enabling operators to curtail lower-priority workloads or migrate jobs between facilities [106, 107]. The uptime target modeled in this analysis assumes a naively dispatched, non-reactive load, and should therefore be interpreted as a conservative lower bound. Facilities leveraging the operational flexibility afforded by storage would in practice achieve higher effective reliability. Battery modules at mid-scenario replacement retain a high state-of-health (89% on average) suitable for redeployment in grid services, arbitrage, or power quality applications, though we omit this residual value from our analysis.

The economic case for microgrids arises from the speed premium, which results from the high value of AI compute. Our baseline value is likely a floor for the internal utility of a chip-hour. It also reflects contemporary hardware – more computationally efficient and higher-performance chips provide more services per unit time and energy. As computing and model capabilities increase, so too does the speed premium.

Data center firms demonstrate revealed preference for deployment speed, co-locating with power generation and acquiring PPAs for aging or retired power plants. However, the number of idled nuclear reactors is finite. While firms can rely on spare capacity and rental gas turbines in the near-term [10, 11], continued buildout will eventually exhaust these resources. Previous operational commitments[108, 109, 110] may further constrain their choice of power source.

Energy demand to serve new data centers will require new grid supply and delivery infrastructure, and without new policy processes to allocate costs to data centers, this new infrastructure will likely be financed by the base of ratepayers. Given the high value of speed, data centers that supply their own power and recapitalize local infrastructure may merit an expedited process for the remaining permitting [111]. Because firms often turn to self-supply in response to interconnection delays, deployment timelines and policy will shape whether AI demand stays on the shared grid or shifts to a parallel, self-supplied system. Such a shift may carry longer-term consequences for the cost, reliability, and environmental footprint of the broader power system that extend beyond the facility-level economics we model here.

Data Availability

All input data derive from publicly available sources: NSRDB PSM4 solar resource data [82], NLR Annual Technology Baseline cost data [88], NLR solar and storage cost breakdowns [89], the PNNL energy storage cost database [92], EIA Annual Energy Outlook turbine costs [93], and grid interconnection queue durations [13]. Processed per-location result tables and the configuration files specifying all model parameters are available in the public repository: https://github.com/acnewkirk/AI-Datacenter-Microgrid-Analysis.

Code Availability

The technoeconomic model, including all power-flow, dispatch, degradation, and optimization code used in this study, is publicly available at https://github.com/acnewkirk/AI-Datacenter-Microgrid-Analysis under an MIT License. The repository includes a notebook (notebooks/reproduce_paper_figures.ipynb) that reproduces the main-text figures from the shipped result tables. Reproducing the full per-location sweep requires a no-cost API key from the NLR Solar Resource API to obtain typical meteorological year data for arbitrary U.S. locations.

Supplementary Information
Speed-to-Power Dominates Energy Costs for AI Data Centers: Technoeconomic Analysis of Powering AI in the Continental United States

S1 Comprehensive SI Methods

We evaluate microgrid feasibility through technoeconomic simulation of complete power systems serving identical datacenter loads. We apply a common operational scenario: a specific number of GPUs requiring continuous power at a target location, then determine the minimum-levelized-cost configuration within each power architecture class that can meet this demand at required minimum annual uptime across the lifespan of the facility.

The analysis proceeds in three stages. First, we establish the hourly facility load that any power system must serve, combining IT demand with location-specific cooling requirements. Second, we simulate candidate power systems meeting this load profile, tracking hourly energy flows from generation through storage and conversion to final consumption. Third, we search each architecture’s design space to identify configurations that minimize levelized cost while delivering required reliability.

This framework enforces scenario equivalence: all power systems face identical hourly demands across the same 25-year evaluation period at the same geographic location. We evaluate four candidate power systems: AC-coupled solar+storage, DC-coupled solar+storage, natural gas with backup diesel, and interconnection to the local electric grid as a baseline.

To establish this scenario, we accept location (lat/long coordinates), required annual facility uptime, and quantity of GPUs as specified inputs. Location-specific climate data are taken from typical meteorological year (TMY) sourced from the National Solar Resource Database (NSRDB) public API. TMY datasets are statistically representative hourly weather sequences derived from multi-decade observations that capture seasonal and diurnal patterns while excluding extreme outliers.

We compare each system in simulation year 27, end-of-life for the PV modules (25 year lifespan), with a base-case discount rate of 7%. For scenarios with BESS, we assume one single end-of-life replacement of the battery modules occurring at the conclusion of operational year 13 (see the battery degradation subsection for more detail). All financial values are in 2022 dollars, and all discounting occurs mid year.

All software is implemented in Python, and all tools are available from the public github repository at https://github.com/acnewkirk/AI-Datacenter-Microgrid-Analysis/tree/main. Our work builds upon two existing open-source tools: NLR’s BLAST-Lite optimization framework [112] and the cost calculator developed by OffGrid AI [81]. Each provided critical starting points for the development of this work. To conduct the geographic analysis, we generated a hexgrid tiling of the continental United States, encompassing 4,317 individual hexagons. For each hexagon, we performed a full simulation at the center point of the hexagon for each microgrid architecture, assigning the resulting values to all points within that tile.

The following section begins with how we construct the IT facility load profile. We then detail how we design and simulate each of our candidate power system. We conclude with the techno-economic assessment and system optimization approaches.

S1.1 Facility Modeling

Our facility model builds from the IT out, following established bottom-up datacenter modeling approaches [113, 114]. We base IT demand on 8-GPU Nvidia H100 DGX nodes, drawing from empirical characterization of these systems during training workloads [115]. Each node exhibits average power draw of 7.3 kW and maximum draw of 8.5 kW, inclusive of memory and interconnect components. The load encompasses compute nodes, embedded networking, and management systems, but excludes cooling and power conversion losses addressed in subsequent sections.

We model aggregate hourly AI training load as baseload demand with minimal variation (±8% random noise around unity), representing 8,760 hours of continuous operation [62]. This scenario can be conceptualized as one continuous training run involving all facility nodes, or alternatively as a facility with mixed workloads performing jobs under optimal scheduling and saturating demand. This training load shape is an idealization of practical facility operations, but serves as a conservative limiting case. The framework accepts alternative load profiles and hardware specifications through modular inputs: node-level power parameters (average and maximum draw), hourly demand patterns, and total GPU count. While our current implementation assumes uniform load distribution across all nodes, the modular architecture readily supports extensions for heterogeneous fleet modeling.

Facilities with a more strongly diurnal usage pattern or greater time flexibility in execution have shown potential in recent work to employ demand response for cost savings and effective capacity expansion [39, 106]. Our modeled scenario provides a conservative bound on microgrid viability. Systems that perform well under inflexible baseload will show improved economic performance with operational flexibility under relaxed constraints.

We allocate the chip-quantity input into 8-GPU servers, that each have the power ranges described above. We construct an expected facility IT load by taking the product of our baseload demand time series, the average node power, and the quantity of nodes. This represents the expected power that must be delivered to the IT hardware in hour. We define the facility modeled maximum IT power demand as the sum of the node maxima. Datacenter operators typically contract with utilities for capacity that reflects the maximum theoretical facility demand. Similarly, power delivery infrastructure, both within and outside the fenceline, is scoped to accommodate this upper-bound value, even though average demand is much lower. This is a common feature of power systems design; infrastructure is built for peak demand, but then amortized over the typically lower level of average utilization.

The peak-provisioning principle fundamentally shapes the economics of both grid-connected and islanded facilities. To meet peak loads, operators must invest in infrastructure capable of handling maximum theoretical demand, even if this capacity sits idle during normal operations. We therefore define a facility design load representing the maximum instantaneous power the infrastructure must deliver:

Pdesign=Nnodes×Pnode,max×PUE99×αcontingencyP_{\text{design}}=N_{\text{nodes}}\times P_{\text{node,max}}\times\text{PUE}_{99}\times\alpha_{\text{contingency}} (S1)

where NnodesN_{\text{nodes}} is the number of compute nodes, Pnode,maxP_{\text{node,max}} is the maximum node power (8.5 kW), PUE99\text{PUE}_{99} is the 99th percentile PUE value, and αcontingency=1.05\alpha_{\text{contingency}}=1.05 represents an engineering margin for component failures. This design load, distinct from average operational load, establishes power system sizing requirements that drive capital costs across all architectures.

S1.1.1 Cooling

Datacenter cooling systems must reject heat equal to IT power consumption plus infrastructure losses, with efficiency varying substantially by technology and climate. Lei and Masanet found that the energy consumption of a given cooling technology can vary by up to 60% location to location[116]. We model location-specific cooling efficiency using hourly PUE values, capturing how ambient conditions affect the availability of free cooling and mechanical system performance throughout the year.

Cooling system performance varies with climate: mechanical-only systems show low geographic variation while free-cooling systems exhibit PUE ranges from 1.05 to 1.4 depending on ambient conditions. The rising heat density of AI chips increasingly favors liquid cooling systems, both direct-to-chip and immersion [117, 118, 119, 120], with future server configurations requiring such systems [121]. Following industry practice for high-density deployments, we exclude configurations with insufficient cooling capacity or prohibitively costly low performance.

We consider six candidate cooling configurations for our modeled facility: (1) IT liquid cooling with waterside economizer; (2) IT liquid cooling with adiabatic-assist air-cooled chiller; (3) IT liquid cooling with dry-cooler air-cooled chiller; (4) air-cooled IT with air-cooled chiller, airside economizer, and adiabatic cooling; (5) air-cooled IT with water-cooled chiller, airside economizer, and adiabatic cooling; and (6) air-cooled IT with air-cooled chiller and airside economizer. These systems align with the cooling distribution modeled for AI-specialized facilities by [114]. Each system’s cooling efficiency and capacity depends on local climatological conditions, specifically dry-bulb temperature and ambient humidity.

We construct an hourly time-series of location-specific climate and weather data relevant to cooling performance (dry-bulb temperature and ambient humidity) from the TMY for the input location. Using Lei and Masanet’s empirically calibrated datacenter cooling system model [116], we pre-compute PUE values for each cooling technology across the range of ambient conditions, creating lookup tables indexed by dry-bulb temperature and humidity. We then build hourly PUE performance profiles of the candidate configurations for the specified location. We assume firms select the cooling configuration with the lowest average PUE value over the year because operational energy use dominates total-cost-of-ownership in cooling infrastructure [122].. We acknowledge that in practice, firms select cooling according to a variety of decision variables, including familiarity, vendor relationships, and compatibility with existing staff expertise and capital equipment. We then combine the hourly IT-load with this hourly PUE to construct an hourly facility load.

The integration of cooling load illustrates the core design principle of scenario equivalence. For a specified quantity of chips and location, the amount of power that must be delivered to the IT and cooling load, and the minimum uptime that design must deliver that power, are held constant in each modeled scenario. Differences in power delivery efficiency affect how much power must be generated at the source to meet that load, and the associated economics, but the energy required by the IT and cooling are constant.

Power demanded by the IT load is the hourly value defined in the previous section, and infrastructure power demand is that value multiplied by the difference between the hourly PUE value and 1. Recall that power infrastructure, both in generation and delivery, is scoped not for the annual average, but for the theoretical maximum. Once we’ve selected a cooling system, we select a design PUE value equal to the 99th percentile PUE produced by the selected system in the modeled year, consistent with industry practice. We then take our maximum IT load, multiply it by this design PUE, and then multiply this product by a scalar design contingency factor αcontingency\alpha_{\text{contingency}} , 1.05 in our base case. This factor corresponds to an engineering margin accounting for unanticipated component failure or malfunctions. This facility design load is the power delivery minimum of our candidate designs for a given facility; any generating system must be able to deliver at least this much power to IT and cooling system.

S1.1.2 Power Systems Architecture

To compare different microgrid systems, we develop candidate power flow models of all paths between generation and facility loads. We address a gap in the existing data center literature by modeling the explicit power distribution system losses of different facility and microgrid architectures. A scenario assumption is colocated generating assets, though the power flow models could be extended to include transmission. We model the individual voltage and current conversion steps within the facility fenceline. Baseline candidate designs are shown in main-text Fig. 2, with the LV topologies shown in S12. Note that we assume islanded natural gas facilities adopt the same power systems architecture as conventional grid-connected facilities, and that the diesel backup generators connect to the facility through the same main transformer. Sensitivity analysis shows that the power-flow pathway of the backup gensets is not significant to facility economic performance due to low annual utilization, so we universally adopt this simplifying assumption.

We model all power systems out from the main LV distribution bus, with the cumulative efficiency of all voltage and conversion steps necessary to each load and from each source. We calculate path efficiency as the aggregate product of all component efficiencies between the bus and the source or load. The component efficiencies, displayed in main-text Fig. 2, are based on component datasheets [77] and operational estimates from industry experts [78]. We discuss optimum-design levelized-cost sensitivity to our choice of component efficiency in the technical parameter sensitivity section of the SI.

Our proposed power-flow paths are consistent with conventional data center design practice [63, 64] or existing all-DC pilots [59, 123]. We assume that the grid baseline and natural gas microgrid follow identical power delivery paths, and adopt the same power-delivery architecture for each, considered from within the facility fenceline. In this baseline power-path, the backup diesel generators are modeled as entering the facility through the same distribution transformer as primary power, and both cooling and IT load are supplied through double-conversion UPS to ensure consistent power quality, an architecture consistent with critical operation baseload facilities [65]. Even if physically collocated, the natural gas turbines do not naively output facility bus voltage, and the power must be gathered and transmit to loads. Exact output voltage is turbine and configuration specific, but is most commonly 13.8 kV for 60 Hz AC. We model a utility step-up transformer which changes voltage for distribution within the on a MV spine at 34.5 kV AC, and then a step-down transformer which then switches either grid or natural gas power down to data hall distribution voltage.

We model PV+Storage systems as using battery storage to provide both facility-scale backup power and uninterruptible power services. These architectures replace diesel backup generators and standalone UPS components with grid-scale Lithium-Iron-Phosphate (LFP) battery modules. Our power system designs follow typical microgrid models that utilize centralized generation and storage. Distributed generation and storage is also viable alternative proven in other applications [79], but is not considered in our baseline case. Component efficiencies are based on the averages of efficiency curve data from [53, 48]. We consider both low-voltage (LV) power distribution and medium-voltage (MV) distribution spine with individual data halls as LV spurs off of this MV bus.

The most efficient distribution topology keeps all assets on a single low-voltage bus: PV, BESS, IT, and cooling co-located, with no MV gathering stage and its attendant step-up/step-down conversions. We model this as a modular containerized design. This LV module would be ampacity bound: the maximum current a single LV bus and its protection can carry, and the maximum wiring length over which PV strings can be gathered at acceptable resistive loss. Taking the 800 V DC data-hall consistent with the emerging OCP standard and a representative per-feeder continuous ampacity of 1,250 A (values consistent with commercial off the shelf cabling), a single LV bus carries 800​V×1,250​A≈1​MW800~\text{V}\times 1{,}250~\text{A}\approx 1~\text{MW} of combined IT and cooling load with its proportionate share of co-located PV and BESS. In the MV cases, the embedded battery sits on its own busway off the switchgear, sized to deliver up to 1 MW of discharge power to the load it backs up; charging is routed through the main switchgear, whose solid-state protection is rated to 2 MW (consistent with the 2.5 kA interrupting capability of available DC breakers). No individual LV channel carries more than 1 MW.

In the low-voltage AC microgrid system, we model a ground-mount solar array with outputs combined through 500 kW central inverters that output three-phase 480 V AC. The storage is a set of centralized battery banks within close proximity, AC-coupled to the switchgear though grid-forming 500 kW battery inverters. Wires are sized to minimize wire loss within reasonable cost. In the medium voltage case, we model 4 MW centralized inverters that feed the step-up transformer. The AC power supply unit (PSU) is a Platinum-rated 10.2 kW 240 V AC to 48 V DC power-factor correction (PFC) rectifier, integrated into each Nvidia DGX H100 node as four plus two redundant 3300 W rectifier modules. The integrated chip-level power electronics then switch the PSU voltage down to the internal chip voltages The cooling load (HVAC, chiller, and pumps) all high performance AC induction or brushless DC motors, powered by an AC variable speed drive (VSD) or a DC electronic speed controller (ESC). Here, we only model the losses of the AC/DC PFC rectifier stage within the VSD, as the DC/AC motor inverter stage is present in all topologies. Power quality and any training induced power transients in the AC systems are managed by the UPS or the BESS components.

The low-voltage DC microgrid topology mirrors the LV AC microgrid. Here we model the solar panels connected with high-power DC/DC power optimizers to DC switchgear. The battery’s DC/DC charge controller handles grid-forming [53] through droop-voltage regulation and coordinates with the microgrid energy management system (MEMS). It distributes power on a ±\pm400 V DC bus. Note that some DC topologies directly connect the battery to the DC bus, but these topologies are out of scope for this study. DC/DC PSUs are required to step the 400 V distribution voltage down to the 48 V of the GPU node. They do not need a rack-mount UPS, and DC VSDs can connect directly to the 400 V bus without need for DC/DC conversion.

A modular campus composed of tiles of these LV busses electrically isolated but interconnected through fiber optic and cooling distribution networks is physically realizable. Such a facility, however, would require hundreds of independently-managed pods, carrying an operational complexity burden. The layout of the campus, dispatching and monitoring across facility, and operations and maintenance would be a substantial undertaking over and above the design challenge. As wide bandgap power electronics continue to mature, we view purely LV systems as viable options for relatively small facilities composed of a few such pods. In light of operational complexity, we consider topologies with MV distribution spines as our baseline architectures.

Given a MV facility, the BESS can occupy distinct positions in the network, trading conversion efficiency against equipment cost and service capability. In our baseline cases, we model centralized storage at a single node in the topology. Note this is an idealization: at facility scale these assets would not sit on one large bus but would be containerized as the scale demands and as power electronics allow. For the purpose of understanding their interface with the network, however, they can be conceptualized as dispatching from a single node. In the AC system the bulk of storage is DC-coupled at the PV field (sharing the PV inverter and charging upstream of it); in the all-DC system it is centralized on the MV-DC spine. In both, a smaller increment of order the nameplate of the load it protects (∼\sim1 MW per LV bus)-is distributed to the data-hall LV buses for local outage ride-through, and in the AC case for grid-forming and load reliability (the effect of this split on modeled cost is low, see sensitivity analysis). Physical factors bound how storage may be redistributed. In the AC topologies, collocating storage and generation to share the inverter requires the battery to be electrically adjacent to PV on the same DC bus, so a distributed PV field could face gathering ceiling on how much storage can be field-coupled. Other storage assets must sit off a spur or at the hall, each forfeiting the shared inverter and buying its own. LV distribution busses have little ampacity headroom for co-located charge/discharge power, and single solid-state DC breakers presently cap at ∼\sim2.5 kA (∼\sim2 MW), so hall-sited storage is constrained to a small share of an islanded fleet that is itself many times facility load.

Storage placed at the data hall provides services: local uninterruptible ride-through, fast transient and fault response local to the load, and, specific to the AC systems, grid-forming voltage and frequency support that must be held physically close to the IT to be effective. These services are real but hard to amortize, since their value accrues as avoided downtime and power-quality assurance rather than energy. We therefore treat the distributed hall increment as a modeled architectural feature whose cost we quantify in the sensitivity analysis while noting its benefits qualitatively.

Our baseline MV cases are detailed in the maintext of the manuscript, but they are repeated here for convenience. Each use a medium-voltage spine to separate centralized generation and storage from the data-hall loads, with individual halls connected as low-voltage spurs; they differ in whether distribution is AC or DC. In the baseline AC microgrid, PV is gathered through central inverters with the bulk of storage DC-coupled at the field (sharing the PV inverter). Power is gathered from the panel strings at 1.5 kV DC, and switched to 1 kV to charge the battery through a bidirectional DC/DC converter. On the shared bus power passes through grid-forming inverters and a step-up transformer onto a 34.5 kV AC spine before stepping down to 480 V three-phase AC at the hall. In the baseline all-DC microgrid, the 1500 V DC PV blocks are stepped up to ±10 kV for campus distribution with the bulk of storage centralized on the MV-DC spine, then stepped down to a ±400 V data-hall bus where the embedded battery’s DC/DC controller provides grid-forming via droop regulation. In both cases a load-matched storage increment (∼\sim1 MW per LV bus) is sited at the data-hall buses for local ride-through, and the centralized storage is modeled as concentrated at a single node for the purpose of characterizing its network interface.
