Here we provide some high-level design heuristics for each PV+BESS architecture, though note the value of ancillary services are not valorized in our core cost model. In the MV DC case, operators should place as much of their storage capacity within the LV data hall as ampacity limits allow. The fewer intermediating components between storage assets and critical loads within the distribution network, the more reliably that node can operate, as there are fewer points of failure to prevent delivery of backup power. Further, DC systems don’t incur the marginal inverter cost penalty (or more accurately, battery converter and management system costs are borne irrespective of site within the topology). Given that the performance of these systems are more sensitive cumulative storage-to-load path efficiency than to PV-to-storage efficiency (see sensitivity subsection), and given that the batteries can provide droop control in the LV hall, DC systems improve in performance as share of batteries on the LV bus increases.

In the AC case, heuristics differ due to marginal inverter costs. PV and BESS are preferably collocated on the same DC bus to share the same inverter. This represents the maximally PV-to-storage path as it avoids any switching losses. It can also avoid inverter clipping losses, allowing otherwise clipped power to be routed to battery charging. In our modeled designs, such savings are marginal to trivial in terms of total system performance. the primary cost lever is thus inverter requirements. While large scale utility inverters on the order of 4 MW can be jointly shared by the panels and storage, once located elsewhere in the network standalone BESS require their own marginal inverters on top of those still required by the generating strings. The grid forming, LV hall level reliability, and power quality benefits of storage assets in the LV hall are non-trivial, so the trade off with inverter costs will be facility specific. Facilities confident that field-side grid-forming holds across the MV spine, and in the distribution network’s reliability for delivering backup power, should site as much storage as possible behind the main inverters; otherwise they should distribute storage into the data hall as needed to provide local grid-forming, reliability, and power-conditioning services.

For each pathway, we calculate cumulative efficiency as the product of all component efficiencies along that path. To determine hourly power requirement at each bus, we divide the IT and cooling loads by their respective bus-to-load efficiencies, accounting for conversion and distribution losses. Similarly, we calculate required generation by dividing bus power by the source-to-bus efficiency for each generation or storage asset. This power flow modeling establishes the core of the facility-specific design constraints: user-specified minimum uptime, location-aware hourly expected IT and cooling demand on the main distribution bus, facility design load for infrastructure scoping, and pathway-specific power delivery efficiencies. Note that we don’t explicitly model supercapacitor banks to maintain bus voltage or any required fault management infrastructure like high efficiency circuit breakers. Full characterization of the costs and performance characteristics of these systems can be found in the sensitivity analysis section of the SI.

S1.2 Generation, Storage, and Degradation

Having established facility demand and power-flow paths, we next model how each generation technology supplies that demand over the project lifetime. Renewable systems must buffer resource intermittency with storage, whereas thermal plants must ride through mechanical failures and maintenance outages. All technologies degrade over time, requiring accurate modeling throughout the evaluation period.

We compare all architectures at year 27,the planned decommissioning point of the solar systems, so that capital recovery periods are aligned even though batteries undergo mid-life replacement and gas turbines operate through continuous maintenance cycles. Using location-specific TMY data, we model hourly solar irradiance and ambient temperature effects on all equipment: PV generation, battery efficiency, and gas turbine thermal derating. Solar-storage systems are simulated with hourly dispatch to capture battery cycling and multi-day weather events. We model natural-gas plants with a probabilistic availability model that reflects forced outages and scheduled maintenance. The following subsections describe the generation, storage, and degradation models in detail.

S1.2.1 PV and BESS

We adopt the vectorized hourly energy balance approach from [81, 46], implemented with a bus-centric architecture that explicitly models conversion losses through different power-flow paths. The PV generation model fetches TMY weather data (irradiance and temperature) for the specified coordinates and feeds these into pvlib’s ModelChain to calculate DC power output. The ModelChain simulates a reference PV module equipped with single-axis tracking, incorporating the CEC temperature model for thermal derating and accounting for 14% system losses from soiling, shading, mismatch, wiring, and light-induced degradation. This simulation runs across all 8760 hours of the year to produce raw DC power values. We then normalize these values by dividing each hourly output by the annual peak DC output, yielding a capacity factor profile ranging from 0 to 1. This can then be rescaled to any specified nameplate capacity.

PV module output is translated to power delivered to the distribution bus with architecture-specific efficiency chains defined in the power-systems subsection. For AC-coupled layouts the chain includes inverter clipping: the effective AC power output from the inverter, PeffectiveP_{\text{effective}}, is defined as the minimum of the efficiency-adjusted DC power produced by the PV modules and the inverter’s nameplate AC output: Peffective=min⁡(PDC×ηinv,Pinverter)P_{\text{effective}}=\min(P_{\text{DC}}\times\eta_{\text{inv}},P_{\text{inverter}}) where PDCP_{\text{DC}} is the instantaneous DC panel output, ηinv\eta_{\text{inv}} is the inverter’s conversion efficiency, and PinverterP_{\text{inverter}} is the inverter’s rated AC capacity. DC-coupled layouts bypass the inverter and use their own conversion stages.

We assume the battery system is composed of 4-hour, 60 MW LFP modules, each rated to store 240 MWh of usable energy [83]. We selected LFP as our storage chemistry due to its excellent durability and ramp rate [84] and current commercial deployment in grid-scale storage applications. While alternate chemistries provide superior energy-density, in the stationary application we model space and weight are not key performance sensitivities. We adopt a conservative LFP round-trip-efficiency (RTE) of 90% [124], and initial battery state-of-energy as 75% nameplate capacity.

Battery capacity fades over time due to calendar and cycling effects, with charge-discharge patterns and depth of discharge affecting fade severity [125, 126, 127]. Battery management systems protect cell longevity by restricting operation to safe voltage ranges, typically utilizing 80-90% of theoretical cell capacity. Our model treats the manufacturer’s nameplate capacity as representing this BEMS-accessible energy window; when we model a 240 MWh battery at 100% state-of-charge, this corresponds to the maximum energy the BEMS permits, not the theoretical cell maximum. This nameplate capacity degrades over time as discussed in subsequent sections.

The hourly dispatch algorithm prioritizes serving facility load from solar generation. Surplus solar charges the battery (subject to power rating and available headroom), with remainder curtailed. Deficits trigger battery discharge (subject to power rating and stored energy). The simulation implements:

Δ​S​O​Et={Psurplus,t⋅Δ​t/(ηcharge⋅Enom)if solar exceeds load−Pdeficit,t⋅Δt⋅ηdischarge/Enomotherwise\Delta SOE_{t}=\begin{cases}P_{\text{surplus},t}\cdot\Delta t/(\eta_{\text{charge}}\cdot E_{\text{nom}})&\text{if solar exceeds load}\\ -P_{\text{deficit},t}\cdot\Delta t\cdot\eta_{\text{discharge}}/E_{\text{nom}}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (S2)

Subject to 0≤S​O​Et≤10\leq SOE_{t}\leq 1 and |Pbatt|≤Pbatt,max|P_{\text{batt}}|\leq P_{\text{batt,max}}. The simulation tracks annual cycles, throughput, curtailment, and unmet load for economic analysis.

Figure S1 traces this dispatch over a representative summer week for the optimized all-DC design at our 100,000-GPU Albuquerque reference site, and makes the energy-constrained character of the islanded design concrete. Peak PV generation exceeds the facility load roughly eight-fold; the battery charges to full within the first hours of sun, the bulk of midday generation is curtailed, and overnight the battery alone carries the load. The gap between the total-load and IT-load traces is the cooling overhead.

S1.2.2 Natural Gas

Natural gas power plant design fundamentally differs from renewable energy system optimization due to its non-linear solution space: multiple interacting discontinuities that preclude simple scaling from reference designs. A gigawatt-scale combined cycle plant represents a fundamentally different engineering solution than what a 100 MW datacenter requires—not merely smaller, but potentially employing a different turbine class, cycle configuration, and redundancy architecture altogether. Turbine selection is inherently discrete, with aeroderivative, F-class, and H-class machines each occupying distinct niches in the capacity-efficiency-reliability design space. The number of units introduces step changes in redundancy and operational flexibility, while the choice between simple and combined cycle configurations fundamentally alters project economics: combined cycle plants approach 60% thermodynamic efficiency but require higher upfront capital investment and extended construction timelines. Our approach addresses these interdependencies by systematically generating candidate configurations from commercially available turbines, applying engineering constraints derived from industry practice, and evaluating the full lifecycle economics of each specific configuration.

Our design tool proceeds from a library of reference natural gas turbines, comprised of 16 individual turbine models, subset according to their manufacturer classification: aeroderivative, F-class, and H-class. These classifications correspond to turbine characteristics: Aeroderivative turbines are flexible but low-capacity and comparatively inefficient; class H turbines have the highest capacity and fuel-efficiency, but are the most complex to manufacture with high upfront costs; F-class turbines are medium-weight, medium capacity frames most often used in industrial applications [128]. For each turbine model, we source nameplate capacity, combustion efficiency, and annual availability from manufacturer specifications and turbine data sheets.

We model the operations of these turbines according to the following formulations. Note that specific parameter values are available in the configuration file of the codebase and the SI. The effective power output and efficiency of any given gas turbine configuration are determined by its class, cc, from the set C={aeroderivative, F-class, H-class}C=\{\text{aeroderivative, F-class, H-class}\}. Performance is a function of scheduled maintenance, operational load, and ambient environmental conditions, which we model as follows:

Periodic maintenance is modeled as a deterministic reduction in a plant’s availability. The Maintenance planned Outage, McM_{c}, for a turbine of class c∈Cc\in C is defined as the ratio of its required annual maintenance period, HcH_{c} (in hours), to the total hours in a year, yy​e​a​ry_{year}.

Mc=Hcyy​e​a​rM_{c}=\frac{H_{c}}{y_{year}} (S3)

A turbine’s thermodynamic efficiency degrades when operating below its nameplate capacity. The adjusted operational efficiency, ηo​p\eta_{op}, is the product of the turbine’s rated efficiency, ηr​a​t​e​d\eta_{rated}, and a class-dependent part-load multiplier, fpart-load​(βo​p,c)f_{\text{part-load}}(\beta_{op},c). This multiplier is a function of the plant’s operational load factor, βo​p\beta_{op}, which is the ratio of average instantaneous power to the plant’s total nameplate capacity.

ηo​p=ηr​a​t​e​d×fpart-load​(β,c)\eta_{op}=\eta_{rated}\times f_{\text{part-load}}(\beta,c) (S4)

The part-load multiplier function is based on empirical analysis of turbine performance curves [129] and is defined as:

fpart-load​(β,c)={1.0−0.10​(1−β)if ​c=aeroderivative1.0−0.15​(1−β)if ​c=F-class1.0−0.20​(1−β)if ​c=H-classf_{\text{part-load}}(\beta,c)=\begin{cases}1.0-0.10(1-\beta)&\text{if }c=\text{aeroderivative}\\ 1.0-0.15(1-\beta)&\text{if }c=\text{F-class}\\ 1.0-0.20(1-\beta)&\text{if }c=\text{H-class}\end{cases} (S5)

A turbine’s maximum power output degrades with higher intake air temperature due to lower density. The available power, Pa​v​a​i​lP_{avail}, is determined by derating the turbine’s nameplate capacity, Pr​a​t​e​dP_{rated}, based on the ambient temperature, Ta​m​bT_{amb}. The derating is governed by a class-dependent factor [130], rderate​(c)r_{\text{derate}}(c), and applies only for temperatures above the ISO standard of TI​S​O=15∘​CT_{ISO}=15^{\circ}\text{C}.

Pa​v​a​i​l=Pr​a​t​e​d×[1−rderate​(c)×max⁡(0,Ta​m​b−TI​S​O)]P_{avail}=P_{rated}\times\left[1-r_{\text{derate}}(c)\times\max(0,T_{amb}-T_{ISO})\right] (S6)

For both capacity derating and part-load efficiency penalty, we selected conservative estimates, and varied the values in sensitivity analysis.

The total power of a combined cycle plant, PC​CP_{CC}, is calculated by augmenting the gas turbine’s power, PG​TP_{GT}, with additional power generated from its waste heat. The power gain depends on the heat of the exhaust gas, which depends on the gas turbine’s efficiency, ηG​T\eta_{GT}, the effectiveness of the heat recovery steam generator, ϵH​R​S​G\epsilon_{HRSG} (assumed to be 80%), and the efficiency of the steam turbine cycle, ηs​t​e​a​m\eta_{steam} (assumed to be 34%) [131].

PC​C=PG​T​[1+(1ηG​T−1)×ϵH​R​S​G×ηs​t​e​a​m]P_{CC}=P_{GT}\left[1+\left(\frac{1}{\eta_{GT}}-1\right)\times\epsilon_{HRSG}\times\eta_{steam}\right] (S7)

Natural gas power plants require a variety of active electrical components to operate, varying from motors to run compressors or cooling water pumps to facility lighting. These loads, collectively termed "auxiliary loads" or less commonly "house loads", draw parasitic power generated by the gas turbine. Importantly what components are necessary for power operation and their cumulative share of nominal turbine output differs by plant configuration [87] . We adopt a configuration specific auxiliary load empirically calibrated to EIA reference plant values [88]

We derive plant performance according to these relationships, with a candidate configurations completely and uniquely determined by: turbine model, fleet size, and single-or-combined cycle. We restrict the design space using industry derived engineering filters to exclude infeasible and implausible configurations.

The most basic is capacity filtering: a plant must be able to meet the facility’s peak demand Pr​e​qP_{req}, defined as PdesignP_{\text{design}} scaled by cumulative power system losses, even under adverse environmental conditions. We enforce this by requiring that the plant’s total capacity, after being derated for the site’s 99th percentile design temperature, be greater than or equal to Pr​e​qP_{req}.

Beyond this physical requirement, we constrain the plant’s annual expected operational load factor (βo​p\beta_{op}) to a window of 30-90%. The 30% floor reflects a conservative minimum stable output level where turbine manufacturer specifications remain reliable. The 90% ceiling enforces an ~11% planning reserve margin, which provides the necessary headroom to handle demand fluctuations or unexpected outages. This margin is a slight relaxation of the 15% standard common in utility planning, reflecting the stable demand profile of the modeled data center.

We impose architectural constraints to ensure that designs reflect commercially viable and operationally practical power plants. First, each plant configuration is limited to a single turbine model, precluding mixed-turbine fleets to reflect the significant logistical and operational challenges of mixed-asset plants. Second, aeroderivative turbines are restricted to simple cycle configurations due to the unfavorable economies of scale of the required heat recovery systems. Finally, to reflect practical limits on plant complexity, the model constrains the number of units in a fleet. This heuristic, based on industry consultation, allows for a greater number of units in fleets of smaller turbines, such as aeroderivatives and small F-class models, than in fleets composed of large industrial frames.

Finally, a more stringent N-1 redundancy filter can be optionally enabled. This standard reliability constraint requires that the plant can still meet the peak demand Pr​e​qP_{req} even with its largest single unit offline. This check is performed using the temperature-derated capacity to ensure N-1 sufficiency during hot weather conditions.

While the engineering filters ensure each plant configuration is robust, we calculate the Expected Unserved Energy (EUE) to quantify the remaining reliability risk and to appropriately size the backup power system. EUE is a standard industry metric representing the expected annual energy shortfall from a given plant design due to both random (forced) and scheduled (planned) outages.

The total EUE is the sum of the forced and planned outage components, E​U​Et​o​t​a​l=E​U​Ef​o​r​c​e​d+E​U​Ep​l​a​n​n​e​dEUE_{total}=EUE_{forced}+EUE_{planned}. We calculate the forced outage component, E​U​Ef​o​r​c​e​dEUE_{forced}, using a binomial probability model based on the single-unit forced availability, AfA_{f}. The expected annual shortfall is the sum of all potential outage states weighted by their probabilities:

E​U​Ef​o​r​c​e​d=Hy​e​a​r​∑k=0N−1(Nk)​Afk​(1−Af)N−k×max⁡(0,Pa​v​g−k⋅Pu​n​i​t)EUE_{forced}=H_{year}\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\binom{N}{k}A_{f}^{k}(1-A_{f})^{N-k}\times\max(0,P_{avg}-k\cdot P_{unit}) (S8)

The planned outage component, E​U​Ep​l​a​n​n​e​dEUE_{planned}, is the deterministic energy shortfall that arises when units are deliberately taken out of service for maintenance. For both forced and planned outages we compute expected unserved energy using the facility’s average demand. For planned outages this implicitly assumes maintenance is scheduled outside the hottest weeks.

Note that EUE is not used as a direct optimization target in our methodology. The primary application of the calculated EUE value is to inform the sizing of the backup diesel system’s fuel reserves. The fuel storage capacity must be sufficient to generate the energy equivalent of the gas plant’s expected annual shortfall, plus a safety margin. This ensures the integrated system can meet its overall reliability target. EUE is an annual statistical expectation, not a chronological simulation. It does not provide information on the timing, frequency, or duration of individual outage events. It serves to size the total volume of backup energy required per year, but not the power capacity of the backup system, which is sized to meet the facility’s peak demand (Pr​e​qP_{req}) .

Unlike the probabilistic treatment of gas plant reliability, diesel backup sizing follows deterministic criteria standard in mission-critical facilities. The diesel system must be able to deliver the full facility demand PreqP_{\text{req}} regardless of the gas plant configuration, as any shortfall would violate the data center’s uptime requirement. We enforce an N+1 redundancy architecture where the total installed fleet includes one additional unit for redundancy. This N+1 configuration ensures the diesel plant can meet full load even with one generator offline for maintenance or failure. Diesel backup system design rules reflect guidance for critical backup power infrastructure [132, 133], with those sources also providing our diesel system financial parameters.

While diesel generators provide the power capacity for backup, their runtime is constrained by on-site fuel storage. We size fuel reserves based on the gas plant’s Expected Unserved Energy, applying a safety factor to account for uncertainty in outage patterns:

Vfuel=max⁡(λ⋅EUEtotal⋅SFC,Vmin)V_{\text{fuel}}=\max\left(\lambda\cdot\text{EUE}_{\text{total}}\cdot\text{SFC},V_{\text{min}}\right) (S9)

where VfuelV_{\text{fuel}} is the fuel storage volume (gallons), λ\lambda is a safety factor (typically 2.0), SFC is the specific fuel consumption (gallons/MWh), and VminV_{\text{min}} represents the minimum code-required storage. The minimum storage ensures 72 hours of runtime at full load, a standard requirement for critical facilities. This dual criterion ensures adequate fuel for both statistical expectations and exogenous scenarios such as extended natural disasters or fuel delivery disruptions.

Note that the tool includes another optional engineering filter that we do not enforce in our base analysis: maximum diesel turbine runtime. Operators are typically only permitted to operate backup power turbines up to some annual limit (typically 200-500 hours, varying by region) per annum due to air quality standards. Above this threshold, operators need to register as prime power providers, with higher operational scrutiny. We elect to not enforce this filter in our base case as the facility in our scenario is a primary power provider, and would thus likely undergo full permitting and regulatory review. If they anticipate their design would require operating the diesel gensets above annual maximum, they would obtain permitting at that initial stage of the process. Users of the tool suite can enforce the flag to filter out designs that would exceed some specified annual max, with the practical impact of favoring multi-turbine configurations.

The diesel backup system we do not independently optimize but rather size deterministically based on the selected gas plant configuration. This coupling means that gas plant reliability directly affects total system costs: a less reliable gas configuration reduces gas plant capital costs but increases both diesel fuel storage requirements and expected diesel consumption. The life-cycle cost optimization described in design optimization subsection captures these tradeoffs, selecting the gas-diesel combination that minimizes total cost while meeting reliability specification.

S1.2.3 Degradation

Power-generating and energy-storage assets degrade over their useful life. Accurate degradation modeling is essential for economic comparison, as systems that appear cost-competitive at commissioning may diverge significantly in delivered energy costs over a 25-year horizon. We implement degradation models calibrated to empirical data where available, with conservative assumptions where data is limited.

For solar PV, we apply a linear degradation model with 1% first-year loss, primarily from light-induced degradation, followed by 0.55% annual degradation thereafter [85]. These degradation values were validated through consultation with a utility solar system design expert. While module-specific and climate-dependent variations exist, the total uncertainty band over 25 years has minimal impact on LCOE due to heavy discounting of later years in financial analysis.

Natural gas turbines experience both capacity and efficiency degradation, with rates differentiated by turbine class to reflect their distinct operational characteristics and maintenance requirements. Properly maintained plants see dramatically lower degradation rates. Our model assumes realistic operating environments with regular maintenance interventions such as compressor washing, resulting in annualized degradation rates that align with industry experience of 0.5-1.5% loss between major overhauls [134]. We differentiate by turbine class, with aeroderivative turbines experiencing higher degradation rates due to their higher pressure ratios and sensitivity to fouling, while F-class and H-class heavy-duty frames exhibit greater durability owing to their robust design and longer service intervals. Importantly, efficiency degradations in natural gas plants affect cost performance but not the system’s ability to deliver SLA-guaranteed power, and capacity degradations remain much smaller than the capacity headroom required by our design rules. This distinction allows us to adopt simplified linear calendar approaches for both PV and gas turbine degradation modeling. See the sensitivity analysis for the discussion of the sensitivity to our choice of degradation factors.

Lithium-ion battery degradation requires more sophisticated treatment. Battery capacity fade results from complex, interdependent electrochemical processes [127] that vary nonlinearly with operating conditions[135]. Depth of discharge (the fraction of battery capacity used in each cycle), C-rate (the charge/discharge rate relative to battery capacity), cell temperature, and state-of-charge (the battery’s current energy level as a percentage of capacity) all influence degradation trajectories. Further, batteries experience both calendar aging (degradation over time regardless of use) and cycling stress (degradation from charge-discharge cycles), and these factors can mutually interact, introducing significant non-linearity into battery fade dynamics.

Battery capacity fade modeling employs BLAST-Lite, an open-source tool implementing semi-empirical degradation models developed by Smith et al. [86]. The tool’s LFP model derives from multi-year cycling data of grid-scale batteries under representative duty cycles, making it directly applicable to our use case. BLAST-Lite tracks degradation through both pathways: calendar aging (time-dependent SEI growth and electrolyte decomposition) and cycle aging (mechanical stress and lithium inventory loss from charge-discharge cycles). The model accepts hourly time-series of power throughput, state-of-charge, and temperature, then computes capacity fade using stress-weighted composite of these mechanisms.

Blast-lite summarizes complex charge-discharge patterns into equivalent stress cycles. For our LFP chemistry, the model represents key empirical behaviors: minimal sensitivity to depth-of-discharge below 80%, accelerated degradation at extreme SOC ranges (>95% and <5%), and Arrhenius-type temperature dependence with roughly doubled degradation rate per 10°C increase. These path-dependent calculations produce more accurate lifetime predictions than simplified equivalent-cycle or calendar-only models.

Our 25-year facility operating lifespan exceeds typical 15-year battery system operating lives, making replacement timing and strategy critical design decisions. While unconstrained optimization might minimize initial capacity and add cells annually to offset degradation, this approach misrepresents actual operational practices, as firms value operational simplicity over theoretical optimality. In theory, an operator could dramatically oversize the initial battery system capacity to provide, in expectation with modeled duty cycle, 25 years of operation above minimum uptime. Such a strategy would be maximally costly, in essence buying idle battery capacity that is undergoing calendar fade that will only see utilization in later years of facility operation. Alternatively, a facility might install the minimum scale battery system capable of achieving y0 uptime, with steady augmentation each year to replace faded capacity. Such a strategy, termed augmentation [136], does not align with data center industry prioritization of reliability and turnkey power systems operation. Existing deployments of large scale energy storage by data centers have been large scale installations with capacity overhang [137, 29, 138].

Overbuilt battery systems still require module replacement to ensure lifetime capacity at reasonable cost. Too early or late a refresh point and the firm is commits to low total usage of the storage assets for one period and greater overbuild for the other. We therefore implement a single full-scale battery replacement in year 13 as an approximation of system midlife, to reflect practical procurement strategies in which facilities execute major infrastructure upgrades as planned capital projects, not continuous optimization exercises. Note that we evaluate the sensitivity to the selection of replacement year in the technical parameter stability sensitivity analysis subsection.

Battery thermal management follows a simplified physics-based approach that tracks temperature evolution throughout the year. We model heat generation from round-trip inefficiency as Qg​e​n=Pt​h​r​o​u​g​h​p​u​t×(1−ηR​T​E)Q_{gen}=P_{throughput}\times(1-\sqrt{\eta_{RTE}}) where throughput power and round-trip efficiency determine waste heat. The battery’s thermal mass (2.3 kWh/°C per MWh capacity) buffers these temperature fluctuations. The thermal mass parameter was derived from a representative 3.9 MWh, 38-ton containerized BESS [139], calculating the system’s total thermal capacitance using mass-weighted specific heat values of its components: 57% LFP cells, 20% steel, and 23% other materials [140, 141, 142].

Active cooling engages when cell temperature exceeds 30°C, with power requirements calculated as the excess heat divided by the cooling system coefficient of performance (derived from the facility PUE). We account for this parasitic load by reducing the facility’s net energy delivery by an equivalent value to the cooling energy use. Though thermal loads could theoretically be scheduled to coincide with solar curtailment periods using batteries, we naively dispatch climate control any hour outside of thermal envelope. The model includes provisions for heating when batteries are idle in cold conditions (below 15°C), this rarely engages in practice. This approach captures the essential thermal dynamics and their impact on both degradation rates and parasitic loads without requiring more detailed modeling.

We conducted initial exploratory data analysis on candidate systems using Blast-lite, revealing characteristics of our usage pattern. Batteries in systems that deliver greater than 90% annualized uptime show only modest fade at their parameterized retirement year, averaging 11% cumulative fade with roughly even total cycle and calendar fade, as shown in S3. Because batteries are sufficient for overnight operations, and because solar panels are sufficient to both deliver facility load during daylight hours and charge the battery for expected overnight energy demand, battery state-of-energy is strongly skewed, with more than a quarter of typical hours spent at 100% SoE, as shown in S2. Typical depth-of-discharge is relatedly modest.

The low battery health degradation we find is consistent with underlying theoretical and empirical results on LFP cycle fade [143, 99]. Islanded PV-plus-BESS systems require significant nominal power overbuild to achieve 90% annual uptime (to say nothing of 2 or 4 9s of reliability) because the sun does not shine at night. The design region is thus energy constrained, not power constrained. Beyond even the storage for a typical overnight load, the battery system must also be scoped to accommodate seasonal ebbs and outlier events.

Systems of this size charge and discharge only a small fraction of their total energy capacity in any given time step. Though the exact value varies design-to-design, the maximum nominal C-rate in a given year is approximately .2, with the average C-rate a third of that. This gentle nominal C-rate is consistent with a low-stress battery operating regime [99].This stressor pattern is also fairly stable year to year: annual throughput cycling increases on average only 11% cumulatively over the life of the battery, mean SoC reduces by 4% on average, and annual thermal load increasing less than 1% on average.

A full Blast-lite call to evaluate every candidate design in the optimization loop would have been computationally intractable. The relatively stable fade regime of our batteries allowed us to address this through gray-box surrogate distillation. The surrogate follows a physics-informed machine-learning strategy: a low-order analytic “scaffold" expresses the dominant aging mechanisms, and a data-driven term learns only the small residual that remains between the scaffold and the simulator output.

We split degradation into calendar and cycle terms:

Δ​qcal=A​tβ​exp⁡(−EcalR​T)​[1+γ​|SOC−0.5|],Δ​qcyc=B​EFCα​exp⁡(−EcycR​T),\Delta q_{\text{cal}}=A\,t^{\beta}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{E_{\text{cal}}}{RT}\Bigr)\bigl[1+\gamma\lvert\mathrm{SOC}-0.5\rvert\bigr],\qquad\Delta q_{\text{cyc}}=B\,\mathrm{EFC}^{\alpha}\exp\!\Bigl(-\frac{E_{\text{cyc}}}{RT}\Bigr),

where tt is elapsed time in years, EFC\mathrm{EFC} is cumulative equivalent full cycles, TT is mean cell temperature in kelvin, and RR is the universal gas constant. We locked the Arrhenius energies at the BLAST-Lite values Ecal=43.3​kJ mol−1E_{\text{cal}}=43.3\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1} and Ecyc=−18.2​kJ mol−1E_{\text{cyc}}=-18.2\;\text{kJ mol}^{-1}. Starting from the BLAST-Lite exponents β0=0.526\beta_{0}=0.526 and α0=0.828\alpha_{0}=0.828, we let the data move them within ±0.25 and fit the scale factors A,BA,B plus the SOC-curvature coefficient γ\gamma. To capture path dependence, we simulated every design through a complete life cycle and recorded each year’s incremental fade. After fitting the scaffold to those increments, we modeled the residuals

r=qBLAST−Δ​qscaffoldr=q_{\text{BLAST}}-\Delta q_{\text{scaffold}}

with a GP that uses a Matérn (ν=2.5\nu=2.5) kernel and a small white-noise term. We assessed accuracy with five-fold grouped cross-validation, treating each design as one group to prevent data leakage.

We constructed a training set out of detailed Blast-lite degradation simulations of candidate systems in 13 locations over a full battery life cycle. These locations included at least one entry in every DOE climate zone in the continental United States, and we simulated 4 designs at each location. Each year’s simulation provided stress features: state-of-charge statistics, temperature, and throughput metrics, creating a path dependent stressor history for each design. Group-aware 5-fold cross-validation ensured robustness across designs and allowed for hyperparameter optimization. We then evaluated the final distilled model performance on a new set of randomly generated designs from 10 locations explicitly not within the training set.

The proxy showed high fidelity to the underlying Blast-Lite simulation: out-of-fold (OOF) mean absolute errors for calendar and cycle fade are 0.0016 and 0.0097 respectively, and each had an R2 greater than 0.99. This proxy maintained predictive performance in our validation data, as shown in S4. The mean cumulative state-of-health error at battery end-of-life between Blast-lite and this proxy is 0.03% for the out-of-sample designs.

We implemented battery fade using static stressor proxies for computational tractability. Rather than modeling the full evolution of stress factors over the battery lifecycle, we approximated degradation using simplified metrics: mean state-of-energy from year zero, and cumulative throughput calculated as year-zero equivalent full cycles multiplied by operating years. While this simplification doesn’t account for evolution in stressors, validation against dynamic stressor models showed minimal accuracy loss: a mean absolute error of only 0.14% state-of-health at end of life. While we initially intended to develop a more complex stressor evolution model, exploratory testing of the y0y_{0} stressors as proxy to provide a performance baseline proved sufficient for accuracy. This static approximation captures the dominant degradation drivers while keeping the optimization computationally manageable, making it well-suited for our large-scale system design exploration.

S1.3 Technoeconomic Analysis

We employ technoeconomic assessment (TEA) to evaluate the financial performance of candidate designs. Using the net power flow models for each system detailed in the previous sections, we associate costs with the construction and operational parameters of each system, discounting future costs into y0y_{0} dollars. We then divide these costs by the cumulative discounted energy production of the system to calculate the levelized cost of energy (LCOE) as shown in S10:

LCOE=∑t=0nC​a​pt+O​pt(1+r)t+0.5∑t=0nEt(1+r)t+0.5\mathrm{LCOE}=\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{Cap_{t}+Op_{t}}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}}{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{E_{t}}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}} (S10)

where tt is the project year, nn is the evaluation year, Ccap,tC_{\text{cap},t} and Cop,tC_{\text{op},t} are capital and operating expenditures in year tt, EtE_{t} is the energy delivered to the IT and cooling loads in year tt (zero before operations begin), and rr is the discount rate. This quantity provides us a direct point of comparison to evaluate the economic performance of different designs. Our base case discount rate is 7%, and we discount mid-year. All values are in 2022 dollars.

Note that LCOE has well-documented limitations when comparing technologies with different operational characteristics such as dispatchability [144, 145], because the metric does not completely capture how generation timing and reliability affect economic value. Our framework explicitly addresses this critique through scenario equivalence: all power systems face identical facility loads, reliability requirements, and geographic constraints, enabling direct comparison of the true cost to deliver equivalent energy services.

For PV+storage systems, capital and operating costs were derived by combining aggregate system projections from [88] with detailed cost decompositions from [89]. The NLR ATB provides bundled utility-scale PV+storage system costs of $2,275/kW (2025, moderate case), which we disaggregated into component costs (PV modules, battery cells, and balance of system) using proportional shares from Ramasamy et al.’s detailed cost breakdowns. To allocate balance of system (BOS) costs between PV and storage components, we compared standalone PV systems to combined PV+storage systems in their data, attributing the full standalone PV infrastructure costs to the solar component and only incremental costs to storage.

For DC-coupled architectures, we estimated BOS cost by analyzing differences between coupling configurations in [146, 89]. While electrical system costs for DC coupled architectures showed marginal increases in [146] due to required DC-DC converters, those costs are exceeded by avoidance of the inverters. In [79] the authors find that scale economies in power systems components result in DC-DC converters having lower capital costs compared to bidirectional AC-DC components. Based on this analysis, we derate DC-coupled solar BoS costs by 29.7% with all savings attributed to reduced PV-side inverter infrastructure while battery-specific BOS costs remained constant. Battery module replacement at year 13 is treated as a capital expenditure using NLR ATB’s projected costs for that future year. Land requirements are parameterized at 4.17 acres per MW of solar capacity [90, 91].

Fixed operating and maintenance costs for PV systems were sourced from Ramasamy et al. [89], using values for standalone PV systems to avoid double-counting battery replacement costs that are embedded in their combined system estimates. We note that these PV O&M costs include inverter replacement, which DC-coupled architectures would avoid; however, as the reference does not specifically decompose costs, we retained the full values while acknowledging this represents a likely small overestimate for DC-coupled systems. Battery storage O&M costs were obtained from the [92] database entry for lithium iron phosphate systems.

Natural gas plant costs vary by turbine class, plant configuration, and capacity. We source baseline capital and operating costs from established references: F-class and H-class single and combined cycle configurations from the NLR ATB [88], and aeroderivative turbines from EIA’s Annual Energy Outlook [93]. These reference plants provide cost benchmarks at specific capacities (e.g., 237 MW for F-class simple cycle, 702 MW for H-class combined cycle).

To estimate costs for configurations that differ from these reference plants, we apply empirical scaling relationships following the well-established “six-tenths rule” [94]. After reviewing component-level scaling behaviors [95], we adopt scaling exponents of 0.67 for capital costs and 0.80 for fixed O&M 11 1 We scale per-kW costs using exponents of -0.33 and -0.20, which is mathematically equivalent to scaling total costs with exponents 0.67 and 0.80 since per-kW cost ×\times capacity == total cost.. The scaling relationships are:

CapExscaled=CapExref×(PplantPref)0.67×fcomplexity\text{CapEx}_{\text{scaled}}=\text{CapEx}_{\text{ref}}\times\left(\frac{P_{\text{plant}}}{P_{\text{ref}}}\right)^{0.67}\times f_{\text{complexity}} (S11)
Fixed O&Mscaled=Fixed O&Mref×(PplantPref)0.80×fcomplexity\text{Fixed O\&M}_{\text{scaled}}=\text{Fixed O\&M}_{\text{ref}}\times\left(\frac{P_{\text{plant}}}{P_{\text{ref}}}\right)^{0.80}\times f_{\text{complexity}} (S12)

where PplantP_{\text{plant}} and PrefP_{\text{ref}} are the candidate and reference plant capacities, and fcomplexityf_{\text{complexity}} accounts for multi-unit configurations not represented in our reference dataset: 1.0 for 1-2 units, 1.3 for 3-4 units, and 1.8 for >>4 units, reflecting increased balance-of-plant and coordination costs. Diesel system costs are linearly scaled according to system capacity from reference documentation [132]. We did not vary variable O&M unit costs within a plant class.

Annual fuel costs in year tt depend on the energy delivered by natural gas and diesel generators, multiplied by their respective fuel consumption rates. Natural gas generation is constrained by plant availability:

EN​G,t=min⁡(Pp​l​a​n​t,t⋅A​F⋅Hy​e​a​r,Er​e​q​u​i​r​e​d)E_{NG,t}=\min(P_{plant,t}\cdot AF\cdot H_{year},E_{required}) (S13)

where Pp​l​a​n​t,tP_{plant,t} is the nameplate capacity after degradation (MW), A​FAF is the availability factor incorporating forced and planned outages, Hy​e​a​r=8760H_{year}=8760 hours represents annual operating hours, and Er​e​q​u​i​r​e​dE_{required} is the facility’s annual energy demand (MWh). Any shortfall is met by diesel generation:

Ed​i​e​s​e​l,t=max⁡(Er​e​q​u​i​r​e​d−EN​G,t,Et​e​s​t)E_{diesel,t}=\max(E_{required}-E_{NG,t},E_{test}) (S14)

where Et​e​s​tE_{test} accounts for mandatory testing requirements. The gas plant’s operating efficiency depends on its operational load factor βo​p=Pa​v​g/Pp​l​a​n​t\beta_{op}=P_{avg}/P_{plant}, which represents the ratio of average facility demand to plant nameplate capacity. Operating efficiency in year tt is adjusted for both part-load penalties and calendar degradation:

ηo​p,t=ηr​a​t​e​d⋅fp​a​r​t−l​o​a​d​(β,c)⋅ηd​e​g​(t)\eta_{op,t}=\eta_{rated}\cdot f_{part-load}(\beta,c)\cdot\eta_{deg}(t) (S15)

where ηr​a​t​e​d\eta_{rated} is the rated efficiency at full load, fp​a​r​t−l​o​a​df_{part-load} is the class-dependent part-load penalty function defined previously, and ηd​e​g​(t)\eta_{deg}(t) represents efficiency degradation over time.

Total fuel cost in year tt is calculated as:

Cf​u​e​l,t=EN​G,t⋅ϱηo​p,t⋅pg​a​s+Ed​i​e​s​e​l,t⋅ηd​i​e​s​e​l⋅pd​i​e​s​e​lC_{fuel,t}=E_{NG,t}\cdot\frac{\varrho}{\eta_{op,t}}\cdot p_{gas}+E_{diesel,t}\cdot\eta_{diesel}\cdot p_{diesel} (S16)

where ϱ=3.412\varrho=3.412 MMBtu/MWh is the thermal energy conversion factor, pg​a​sp_{gas} is the natural gas price ($/MMBtu), ηd​i​e​s​e​l\eta_{diesel} is diesel specific fuel consumption (gal/MWh), and pd​i​e​s​e​lp_{diesel} is the diesel price ($/gal). Diesel price were based on the USA national average according to the EIA circa July, 2025 [147]. We price natural gas at the state level, using an Olympic scored 5-year average of each state’s industrial natural gas price [148]. We analogously assign each state an industrial electricity price based on the July industrial electricity prices [98] All prices are reported in y0y_{0} dollars.

Our LCOE calculation divides total system costs by delivered energy at the facility loads, not generated energy at the source. For solar+storage systems, EtE_{t} represents the hourly facility demand successfully served after accounting for all conversion losses through the power distribution chain. Natural gas plant fuel consumption and equipment sizing reflect required generation at the source, yet we amortize costs only over the energy services delivered to the load, as with the PV based systems. This approach ensures consistent comparison across architectures: all systems are evaluated based on the energy that actually reaches IT and cooling equipment.

S1.3.1 Procurement, Construction, and Interconnection

Beyond equipment and operating costs, project economics depend critically on implementation timelines that vary substantially across generation technologies and grid interconnection pathways. Economic value from any end-use is only unlocked when construction of generation and delivery assets completes. When we refer to construction, we mean the combined site permitting, engineering design, physical construction, testing, and commissioning required to begin plant operation.

We applied the following capital outlay schedule across all architectures: For projects lasting one year or less the entire investment is assumed to occur at notice to proceed (year 0); for two- and three-year builds the schedule follows industry and modeling heuristics of 40 %/60 % and 30 %/40 %/30 % in years 0–2 [93, 149]. Projects longer than three years are treated as being spent uniformly: the total cost is divided equally among the full years of design and construction and prorated for any remaining partial year.

For solar and storage systems, we began with the 2 year all-in timeline from [46]. To validate this assumption, we consulted with relevant industry experts. An early stage grid storage expert estimated that the median time frame for component delivery of a large contract for LFP cathodes was 12 months using the existing mature supply chain. They estimated the time to bootstrap a new production base (for example in response to export restrictions) from scratch would be 18-36 months. A PV systems design expert estimated the average cumulative project timeline for an integrated utility scale PV+BESS project was 18 months, with 16-24 months as the overall range. Based on this feedback, we select 24 months as our cumulative project development timeline to bring solar+storage systems online.

Natural gas plants face more varied timeline influences. We model construction time as differing between single and combined cycle plants, building off estimates in [93], with the additional 2 months for combined cycle configurations reflecting increased plant size and complexity. Natural gas plant construction is not perfectly parallelizable, especially with regard to the keystone component of the turbine. We estimate that 30% plant construction and validation must occur after turbine delivery, making turbine receipt the rate limiting factor. While reports of turbine delays can exceed five year [150], we select value of three years for all turbine models. With base construction timelines of 40 months (simple cycle) and 42 months (combined cycle), total project duration is determined by the maximum of either the base construction time or turbine delivery plus post-delivery construction share.

As a point of comparison, we also estimate the time to interconnection for baseline grid-connected facilities: this includes the initial request processing, any associated studies, and construction of marginal transmission and distribution infrastructure. The process and complexity can differ between supply-side and demand-side interconnection requests, but we lack systematic data for demand side request duration. We adopt supply side interconnection queue data as our proxy for large load interconnection timeline, using raw data from [13]. We took the 2018-2023 median initial-request-to-commercial-operation span among completed projects reported for each ISO/RTO or non-ISO region, converted it to years, and assigned that value to every state in the region. For the handful of states that straddle two regions we chose the higher of the two values. Although based on supply-side projects, these medians provide an empirically grounded proxy for the timeline a large load would expect to interconnect. We examine the sensitivity of our results to these timeline assumptions sensitivity analysis section of the SI.

S1.3.2 Design Optimization

To identify cost-optimal configurations within each architecture class, we must search design spaces while maintaining the hard constraint that all systems achieve required facility uptime. The search strategies differ fundamentally between technologies with continuous versus discrete design variables. Solar+storage optimization searches over continuous capacity ranges for both solar (typically 1-15× facility load) and battery power (typically 1-10× facility load). We employ two-stage optimization: sampling with relaxed evaluation (year-0 only) identifies feasible regions, then differential evolution refines the solution using full lifecycle analysis. Designs that cannot meet minimum uptime in y0y_{0} will not meet minimum uptime at EoL. This approach efficiently handles the non-convex solution landscape created by the interplay between diurnal solar cycles, multi-day weather events, and battery state-of-charge dynamics

In our base case, we treat design increments in PV based systems as effectively continuous, the marginal solar cell or LFP module is minimal compared to the scale of the facility. We test sensitivity to this assumption by evaluating the affect on LCOE of jumping up to the nearest minimum PV and BESS design increment/step size. Sweeps across facility scales (10,000-100,000 GPUs), locations (Phoenix, Austin, Portland), and module sizes (1-10 MW) show cost penalties scale inversely with system size and are dominated by discrete factorization alignment rather than system performance. Median penalty across realistic configurations (2.5 MW PV, 1 MW BESS and below) is <0.3%<0.3\%, though the combination of small facilities (<25,000<25,000 GPUs) and oversized step size (>5>5 MW) can cause the penalty to exceed 2%. We observe the same phenomenon with commercially available power electronics. Taking a 4 MW utility inverter as our example, and based on component costs from our reference case, explicitly modeling inverter increment can increase LCOE on the order of .25% over the continuous case at a 100k GPU facility, with penalties approaching 1% at smaller facilities. Given the small absolute penalty of these industry representative step-sizes ($0.001 / kWh on average) as compared to the continuous optimum, we accept continuous search as a simplifying assumption.

The key computational challenge is avoiding full 25-year hourly simulation for each candidate design. We make two approximations. First, during search we minimize capital cost rather than LCOE for solar and storage systems —these are proportional for systems with identical operational profiles, making capital cost an exact proxy. Second, we evaluate only four anchor years that capture the system’s degradation trajectory: fresh commissioning, maximum degradation before battery replacement (year 13), the discontinuity from replacement (year 14), and end-of-life (year 25). Between anchors, linear interpolation slightly underestimates the generated energy. This causes our method to overestimate LCOE by 0.014% on average, acceptable given the 6-fold reduction in simulation calls.

Natural gas systems present a discrete combinatorial problem: select turbine model, determine unit count, and choose cycle configuration. The engineering filters described previously reduce the solution space sufficiently that exhaustive enumeration becomes tractable. We evaluate LCOE for each configuration passing the filters and select the minimum-cost option. Unlike the continuous solar+storage optimization requiring iterative search, natural gas selection is deterministic once the feasible set is enumerated.

S1.3.3 Value of Energized Compute

Unlike conventional energy infrastructure that generates value only after commissioning, data centers house compute assets capable of generating revenue immediately if deployed elsewhere. Each month of construction represents not only capital carrying costs but also foregone computational output. This opportunity cost varies dramatically across power architectures: grid interconnection may require 4 years in congested regions, translating to 2 years of lost utility compared to faster-deploying alternatives. We term this differential the “speed premium”, the economic value of earlier compute availability. This section develops a framework for quantifying these time-dependent costs and incorporating them into our technoeconomic comparison.

Proper comparison of total system economics requires accounting for both the levelized cost of energy and the opportunity cost of delayed operations. This opportunity cost represents the value of compute services that could have been delivered during the marginal construction period of a slower-to-build system. This necessarily raises the question: what would the value of those computations have been?

Within AI development, GPU-hours represent the fundamental unit of resource allocation, with utilization carefully tracked and optimized. The existence of liquid spot markets for H100 compute provides an empirical lower bound for this value: at $2.40 per GPU-hour [96], operators who cannot extract at least this value from their infrastructure would rationally rent capacity on the open market instead.

Infrastructure providers with internal AI development (such as major hyperscale cloud firms) must ration compute between internal workloads and external rental based on relative value. When internal workload value falls below rental rates, profit-maximizing firms should rent capacity rather than run lower-value jobs internally. The rental price thus represents the marginal decision threshold: the value of the last GPU-hour consumed internally.

We use the observed spot rental price for H100 capacity ($2.40/GPU-hour) as our baseline opportunity cost. This represents a reasonable approximation for hyperscalers who continuously optimize across diverse workloads spanning frontier model training to routine inference and fine-tuning. This assumption likely provides a lower bound for specialized AI labs running exclusively research training workloads. See the sensitivity analysis and Figure 3 in the results for further discussion of how GPU-hour valuation affects results.

We model the value of lost compute during construction years as:

V​L​Ct=∑h=1Hidle,tNGPU×pspotVLC_{t}=\sum_{h=1}^{H_{\text{idle},t}}N_{\text{GPU}}\times p_{\text{spot}} (S17)

where V​L​CtVLC_{t} represents the value of lost compute in year tt, Hidle,tH_{\text{idle},t} is the total idle compute hours in year tt prior to operations, NGPUN_{\text{GPU}} is the total GPU count, and pspotp_{\text{spot}} is the hourly spot-market price per GPU-hour [96]. Only idle hours before the start of operations at topst_{\text{ops}} are considered. We incorporate V​L​CtVLC_{t} into our total cost assessment as:

LCOEadj=∑t=0n(Ccap,t+Cop,t+VLCt)(1+r)t+0.5∑t=0nEt(1+r)t+0.5\text{LCOE}_{\text{adj}}=\frac{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{(C_{\text{cap},t}+C_{\text{op},t}+\text{VLC}_{t})}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}}{\sum_{t=0}^{n}\frac{E_{t}}{(1+r)^{t+0.5}}} (S18)

This formulation treats lost compute value as functionally an additional expense during construction years, ensuring architectures with longer deployment timelines bear the full economic burden of delayed operations. By default the accounting places foregone-compute cost from project initiation onward; alternative schedules can be modeled by adjusting when V​L​CtVLC_{t} becomes non-zero.

Note that indexing V​L​CtVLC_{t} to y0y_{0} is a modeling convenience, not an economic claim: it does not assume a firm procures its GPUs at project start and leaves them idle through construction, a strategy no operator would adopt. The origin is simply the date from which foregone compute is counted, and the comparison is insensitive to it across the relevant range. The quantity that governs architectural preference is the difference in present-value cost between two options, and any opportunity cost accrued before the earliest energization (“go-live”) date is common to all architectures and cancels exactly in that difference, provided the origin falls on or before that earliest date. We could equally index to y2y_{2}, y1.5y_{1.5}, or any date up to the fastest go-live and recover the same ranking.

Because L​C​O​EadjLCOE_{\text{adj}} divides by architecture-specific discounted delivered energy, this common term does not cancel exactly in the ratio, but the residual sensitivity of the ranking to the origin is small relative to the energization-date differential that drives it. Index choice can alter preference order only outside this regime—when chip delivery postdates the fastest go-live, so that the earliest-energizing architecture cannot fully capitalize on its head start. Accordingly, firms with known internal procurement and silicon-delivery timelines should index V​L​CtVLC_{t} to their own schedule.

Figures S7 and S8 apply this framework geographically by inverting the comparison: they map how quickly a grid interconnection (Figure S7) or a natural-gas plant (Figure S8) would have to be delivered to match the speed-premium LCOE of DC-coupled solar at each location.

S1.4 Sensitivity Analysis

We evaluate how parameter uncertainty affects both system costs and architectural selection through two complementary approaches: varying parameters for fixed designs to test cost estimate robustness, then re-optimizing with modified parameters to assess robustness. Within a fixed design, LCOE is linear in each cost parameter, so a one-at-a-time perturbation moves LCOE in proportion to that component’s share of lifecycle cost. Re-optimizing under perturbed parameters can only lower costs with respect to the fixed design response, so the fixed design case upper bounds the re-optimized case.

For our fixed design and cost structure sensitivity sweep, we selected a site in southeastern Colorado (37.5, -103.5) with a local gas price of $7.70 / MMBtu, and tested at 99% facility uptime. We chose this site for its moderately high insolation and moderate natural gas price. Where a perturbation changes the resource or the energy required to deliver a given service (design weather year, network topology, optimization stability), we evaluate sensitivity on multi-site panels spanning the 14 continental U.S. DOE climate zones.

S1.4.1 Baseline LCOE sensitivity

Excluding idling, solar+storage base LCOE responds most strongly to the discount rate (27–28% decrease at 3%, 41–43% increase at 12%). Balance-of-system and year-0 battery cost are next, each shifting LCOE by 4–8% under ±\pm20% variation, followed by module cost (∼\sim3–4%); construction timeline, O&M, and replacement-battery cost are second-order (≤\leq5% on the long-build side, and ≤\leq1.6% for O&M and battery BOS). Land costs are negligible, requiring a 6×\times increase to ∼\sim$1M/km2 to match even battery O&M in cost influence.

Natural gas base LCOE is most sensitive to fuel price, with the continental U.S. range (Oklahoma to California) creating roughly $0.08/kWh variation at the 100,000-GPU scale, larger for smaller turbines. Discount-rate effects are comparable ($0.03–0.05/kWh across 3–12%). Construction timeline and ±\pm20% capital costs each affect LCOE by ∼\sim$0.01–0.02/kWh.

S1.4.2 Speed-premium sensitivity

Incorporating deployment speed dramatically amplifies temporal parameter influence. For solar+storage, discount rate and GPU opportunity cost ($1.00–4.00/hr) each create $0.55–0.60/kWh swings in LCOEadj\text{LCOE}_{\text{adj}}—larger than construction-timeline effects (∼\sim$0.38/kWh). Natural gas shows even stronger sensitivity (GPU idling ∼\sim$1.36/kWh, discount rate ∼\sim$1.22/kWh, construction timeline ∼\sim$0.89/kWh) due to its longer baseline timelines. At current GPU rental index values, deployment speed dominates nameplate energy economics.

As a complementary check on the robustness of our estimates of which of our modeled architectures has the lowest LCOEadj\text{LCOE}_{\text{adj}}, we compute a pairwise indifference envelope across all 4,317 valid hexes at 100,000 GPUs: a hex is flagged as contested if its second-cheapest architecture (among AC-Coupled MV solar, DC-coupled MV solar, grid-connected, and NG) falls within 1 ¢/kWh of the lowest cost option. We selected this value as an arbitrary reporting threshold rather than any data-derived breakpoint. Under the baseline 4-year gas build, 149 hexes (3.5%) are contested, all at the solar–grid boundary; NG never enters the envelope. In the accelerated 3-year NG case, the count of near indifferent tiles climbs to 348 hexes (8.1%), with the new mass split roughly evenly between DC-solar-preferring and NG-preferring hexes (168 vs. 136 respectively; the remaining 64 are grid). In both cases contested hexes are a small minority, and the contested hexes do not skew systematically toward any particular technology as runner up.

S1.4.3 Fuel-price volatility

Natural-gas LCOE inherits delivered fuel-price volatility, but the magnitude of that exposure is fixed at design time by the plant a facility can economically build, which is in turn bounded by its scale. For a representative city in each continental DoE climate zone and at three facility scales, we size the cost-optimal gas plant at the state’s baseline gas price, then recompute its LCOE under a set of alternative delivered fuel-price levels (Figure S10); the slope of LCOE against fuel price is the facility’s committed fuel-price elasticity. No design response to price is permitted: each plant is a price-taker on its installed heat rate.

Elasticity is governed by the installed heat rate, and the accessible heat rate is gated by scale. Small and mid-scale facilities (15,000 and 75,000 chips, ∼\sim20 and ∼\sim100 MW) draw aeroderivative simple-cycle plants almost everywhere, with an elasticity near 0.0116 $/kWh per $/MMBtu that is nearly independent of location. Combined cycle, with its lower heat rate, becomes the cost-optimal choice only at sufficient scale (135,000 chips, ∼\sim180 MW) and only where mean gas prices are high enough to amortize its larger capital cost. When selected it flattens the elasticity. Because combined cycle appears only at the largest scale in our sweep, scale and architecture are collinear.

Elasticity sets how LCOE moves per unit of fuel-price change; the realized spread also depends on how much prices actually move. To bound the latter we run a complementary analysis on the 48 contiguous states at three scales (10k/75k/300k chips), drawing plant-lifetime fuel-price paths by stationary block bootstrap (Politis–Romano, mean block 12 months; 2000 paths) from each state’s post-2010 monthly industrial series, sizing the plant once at the bootstrap-mean price and running the fixed plant over every path. Historical fuel-price dispersion moves NG LCOE within a P5–P95 band of roughly $0.005–$0.024/kWh (median cell ∼\sim$0.011/kWh), with no shift in the central estimate—LCOE is linear in fuel price, and the bootstrap mean reproduces the deterministic mean-price LCOE to within 0.2% in every cell. The band narrows with scale (median $0.0139 →\to $0.0110 →\to $0.0084/kWh from 10k to 300k), consistent with the elasticity result: larger facilities draw lower-heat-rate plants, so each delivered kWh carries less fuel cost and less fuel-cost dispersion.

The practical consequence is that the design-time option to blunt fuel-price exposure by building a more efficient plant is available only to sufficiently large facilities; smaller deployments are locked into the more fuel-exposed simple-cycle regime. Two caveats. First, this is purely a design-time option: once built, every facility is a price-taker on its installed heat rate, the regime the figure depicts. Second, this cost-side sensitivity is generally second-order relative to the speed premium that dominates the cross-architecture comparison.

S1.4.4 Technical parameter stability sensitivity

Re-optimization with modified technical parameters shows robust architectural selection. For natural gas, 72 parameter variations across four scales triggered only five configuration changes, all from power electronics efficiency improvements reducing generation needs across turbine size thresholds. Technical parameters (part-load curves, temperature derating, conversion efficiencies) show 1–3% LCOE impacts when relevant to selected configurations. Solar systems exhibit comparable stability, with battery round-trip efficiency largest (about −2.6%-2.6\% to +3.2%+3.2\% over the 0.85–0.95 range) and power conversion ±\pm1–3%. Sizing to meet end-of-life availability requirements effectively eliminates design contingency sensitivity: under common random numbers the re-optimized design is unchanged across the 1.03–1.10 range, leaving no first-order cost impact. In five instances, the design optimization for natural gas systems switched to a different configuration when changing a power electronics value. In each case, high-end estimates for UPS or PSU efficiency enabled a lower-capacity design to pass the minimum load engineering filter.

Variation in the modeled battery replacement year (16 and 10 years vs. the 13-year baseline) shifts LCOE by −0.61%/+5.10%-0.61\%/+5.10\% for AC-coupled systems and −1.14%/+3.48%-1.14\%/+3.48\% for DC-coupled systems. These cases are re-optimized with the degradation schedule re-anchored to the replacement year, so both the discounted timing of the replacement capital outlay and a modest re-sizing of the battery contribute: the optimal battery capacity shifts by a few percent across the range, with a later replacement requiring somewhat more initial storage to hold reliability at the more-degraded pre-replacement year.

The battery replacement vs augmentation strategy that likely best balances cost and operational objectives would be fixed period augmentation, replacing only faded capacity once or twice over the facility lifespan but continuing to operate existing batteries, with tests of such augmentation strategies reducing costs by 8% compared to the fixed replacement strategy. Such savings are notable, and make theoretical sense given the high SoH of these BESS systems at modeled replacement year. We should tread lightly in our interpretation however, as our modeled system lifespan exceeds the operational history of utility scale LFP systems in wide commercial deployment. To remain within in the duty cycle distribution our fade model is built on, and in light of known industry reliability preference and operational caution, we hold replacement year (and system replacement rather than augmentation) fixed while acknowledging this conservative assumption raises baseline costs of our BESS based systems.

S1.4.5 Network topology and storage placement

Beyond the component-efficiency sensitivities above, we assess how the power systems choices within the PV+BESS architecture (distribution voltage, where storage sits, and load conditioning). Unless noted, topology deltas are reported on base LCOE for a 100k-GPU MV facility; the medium- vs. low-voltage comparison spans all 4,317 hexes, while the placement, path-value, and conditioning analyses use a 14-site panel spanning the DOE climate / solar-resource range (best-of-five re-optimization per site). Table S4 orders these by magnitude: a single first-order lever (whether the full IT load is conditioned online) and a set of second-order siting choices whose AC cost reduces to whether storage rides the shared PV inverter. The text reports the panel ranges that establish robustness. In the MV DC case, siting nodes include within the data hall or off the main MV distribution feeder bus, or direct coupled to the PV. In the AC case, storage could be placed DC coupled with the PV behind the inverter, or within the data hall (or off the MV spine) with their own dedicated inverter. In each case, there is a dominated option: MV coupling strictly outperforms direct coupling to the PV in the DC architecture. In the AC architecture, data hall embedded is strictly preferred to MV spur. In our discussion of topological choices we will discount those nodes moving forward, see S12.

Across the full geographic sample, the MV architecture costs +3.7% (AC) and +2.4% (DC) more in median LCOE than the single-bus modular LV architecture. This delta is the added conversion loss of the MV design. Composition differs by architecture: for the all-DC system it is purely the two MVDC spine crossings, whereas for the AC system it also includes the discrete MPPT and battery DC-DC stages that accompany field DC-coupling of storage as well as marginal inverter requirements if hall embedded. The LV architecture is therefore modestly cheaper where physically realizable, but, as established in the Power Systems Architecture section, it is bounded by practical limits of fault current, bus and component ampacity limits, and PV gathering line losses.

For each of the MV designs, we quantify the cost of siting all storage at each candidate node by holding the optimized baseline design fixed, varying the distribution of storage placed at different nodes at the network (e.g. 70% in the data hall, 30% behind the solar inverter, etc.) adjusting the total PV and BESS capacity to return exactly to the threshold uptime constraint, and measuring the change in total system costs. For the all-DC system the discharge-weighted pull is toward the load: across the 14-site panel, relative to the spine baseline, all-field storage costs +0.7 to +1.4% and all-hall −-0.8 to −-1.5% (medians: +1.0% and −-1.2%), a tight band across the full climate range. The hall position is cheapest but ampacity-strained—charging the islanded battery fleet can draw 7–16×\times facility load while the hall LV buses admit only a few percent of it—so the realized benefit is negligible and, once the ampacity cap is applied, the spine fed centralized storage baseline is within ∼\sim0.05% of the cost optimal embedded LV BESS case. Because the all-DC system has no AC waveform to form, nothing forces storage to the hall, and DC placement is effectively closed.

For the AC system, relocating storage off the field forfeits the shared PV inverter; the resulting re-inversion cost is additive in the relocated share. We price it conservatively at the full avoided PV-side inverter bundle, $253/kW (the AC−-DC solar-BoS differential of the TEA cost model). Provisioning the distributed hall increment—of order one facility-nameplate of storage, ≈\approx10% of the islanded fleet—then adds a re-inversion capital cost of +0.5 to +1.3% of LCOE across the sweep (median +0.83%).

A complementary fixed-design analysis (improving one power-flow path by one percentage point and re-shrinking the fleet to achieve equivalent energy services) finds the battery discharge path is the dominant cost lever in every architecture and climate. Each percentage point improvement in cumulative path efficiency of battery-discharge-to-load is worth 0.7–0.9% of system costs across the 14-site panel (median 0.78%). This is roughly 2–4×\times the charge path and well above the solar-to-load path. This ordering is robust to supply strategy: walking the solar/battery ratio across a four-fold range along the 99%-uptime frontier leaves discharge sensitivity essentially flat. PV-to-battery-charge sensitivity rises with battery-heaviness, from near-zero in solar-heavy, heavily-curtailed designs to ∼\sim0.5% in battery-heavy ones. The practical implication is that the cost exposure of the power system concentrates on the storage discharge chain (the battery converter, the inverter, and the switchgear) regardless of the optimal design being solar- or battery-driven.

The our baseline LV and MV AC architectures maintain power quality through grid forming and do not fully condition all IT load to manage training transients. We separately quantify the cost of full double-conversion conditioning: routing the entire IT (and optionally cooling) load through an in hall BESS uninterruptible power supply. We apply the double-conversion factor (0.94) to the AC bus-to-load path and re-optimizing. This is the most cost consequential choice in distribution architecture for costs: across the 14-site panel, full IT conditioning adds +5.6% to +6.2% to base LCOE (median +5.9%). Conditioning IT and cooling together +6.1% to +6.7% (median +6.4%). The penalty is climate-invariant (it varies by under a percentage point across resource regimes spanning all DOE climate zones) with at most a mild (∼\sim0.5 pp) tendency to be lower in cold, low-solar climates, near the run-to-run optimization noise. Whether such conditioning is a genuine requirement (and for IT alone or IT and cooling) is an operational decision [151], not a model output; we report its cost conditionally so that a reader requiring fully-conditioned power can locate the corresponding architecture and premium.

Finally, we decompose the all-DC advantage itself into a path-efficiency component and a capital component. They contribute in roughly equal measure. The efficiency side reflects that the DC chain delivers more of the generated energy to the load: roughly 90% of PV output reaches the IT load versus 83% for the AC chain. The cumulative battery-charge-discharge-IT load sees comparable savings for the DC architecture over AC. Holding capital costs equal, these efficiency improvements are worth ∼\sim7.9% of LCOE. The capital side is the avoided PV-side inverter and AC collection equipment (∼\sim$253/kW of solar balance-of-system), a further 7.5–9.3%, larger where the optimal design runs more PV-heavy since the saving accrues per kW of PV. Composed at fixed design, these components predict a 15–16% advantage, modestly below the 18.3% mean across the re-optimized continental sample at the 100,000-GPU scale. The difference reflects the sizing response, as higher path efficiency also reduces the overbuild required to meet the reliability constraint. This decomposition makes the advantage robust to uncertainty in DC conversion-equipment pricing. Holding optimized designs fixed, the DC-side solar BoS must reach $965–1,176/kW (1.6–2.0×\times our central estimate, and 13–38% above the corresponding AC-system BoS) in our range of evaluated designs before the all-DC advantage vanishes entirely. This would require the DC-specific power-conversion equipment to cost more than the entire avoided inverter bundle.

S1.4.6 Optimization stability

To characterize the robustness of our designs and the stability of the optimizer, we run 24 independent optimizations at each of 14 locations spanning the DOE climate zones, for the DC-coupled architecture serving 100,000 GPUs at 99% uptime on the medium-voltage spine (design load ≈\approx130 MW, varying modestly with cooling performance). Across locations the LCOE coefficient of variation ranges from 0.1% to 4.7% (median 1.0%, mean 1.4%) and varies with climate: high-solar-resource sites (Miami, Phoenix, Las Vegas, El Paso) converge tightly (CV <0.35%<0.35\%), while humid or variable-resource climates (Northern Virginia, Houston, Atlanta) are the loosest (2.7–4.7%). Figure S9 shows four representative climates, with Albuquerque and Denver at the tight end and Baltimore and Chicago more dispersed.

Component sizing varies substantially more than LCOE. Across the 14 sites the solar-capacity CV has median 5.3% (mean 5.5%, up to 10%) and the battery-capacity CV median 6.9% (mean 6.3%, up to 11%), several-fold the LCOE CV. This disparity indicates a near-flat objective basin—configurations differing by 5–10% in component sizing achieve nearly identical cost (within ±\pm2% LCOE). This Pareto frontier-like behavior reflects substitutability between solar and battery capacity on the margin near the boundary of the uptime constraint.

Cross-location differences reflect search difficulty rather than a change in problem structure. Where solar resource is abundant and steady, the cost-optimal region is a large target that sampling-based optimization reliably finds; where resource is variable, that region is narrower or split into local basins, lowering the chance a random seed initializes near the global optimum. The figure shows this directly: easy locations cluster tightly along a clear trade-off curve, while harder locations mix dense clusters (converged) with interior points (suboptimal convergence) carrying 2–3 cents/kWh penalties

For challenging locations (CV >2%>2\%), running 3–5 independent optimizations and selecting the minimum provides more reliable results. Alternatively, increasing the differential evolution iteration budget from 25 to 50–100 generations improves convergence at modest computational cost for detailed investigation of specific candidate sites.

S1.4.7 Design-year weather sensitivity

Our main analysis sizes each design against a single typical meteorological year (TMY), which raises two questions: is a TMY a biased basis for design, and how much does a design’s cost depend on the particular weather year chosen? We re-optimized the DC-coupled architecture against the TMY and against each of the fourteen historical years 2010–2023 (drawn from the NSRDB, our weather source throughout). We chose two cities in each of the fourteen DOE climate zone modelling 40,000 GPU facilities and 99% uptime, taking the best-of-five seeds per design. We draw inference per location, Figure S11 pools the resulting single-year deviations across all location-years to show their shape.

Relative to the distribution of historical years, TMY is a mildly optimistic design basis, with the optimism concentrated in the tail rather than spread across the bulk. The pooled single-year deviations (Figure S11) are right-skewed: most years sit close to the TMY value, but a thin upper tail of punishing years pulls the mean to +$0.0121+\$0.0121/kWh above TMY. Within a site, the across-year LCOE distribution is right-skewed at 23 of 28 locations (mean per-location skew +0.68+0.68, p<10−4p<10^{-4}), and across locations the historical-year mean exceeds TMY by a median of 4.5% (mean 3.0%); a location-clustered robust test places the mean TMY shortfall at $0.012/kWh (p=0.024p=0.024), with TMY the cheaper basis at 20 of the 27 sites. Because the gap is a tail effect and not a uniform offset, TMY closely tracks the typical (median) historical year, and trimming design years beyond ±2\pm 2 standard deviations from the mean removes the significance of the bias: TMY misses the worst years rather than systematically diverging from the typical one.

This tail-driven optimism nonetheless leaves TMY the preferable single-year basis for designing systems. A uniformly drawn historical year is unbiased for the across-year mean by construction, but its draw-to-draw scatter is large: the single-year LCOE has a per-location standard deviation around the mean of 11.5%11.5\% (median across sites). TMY, a deterministic construction near the typical year, carries essentially no sampling variance, so its error is the ∼5%\sim 5\% bias alone. As point estimators of the across-year mean cost, a single random year is therefore roughly 2.2×2.2\times noisier (RMSE 11.5% vs. 5.2%) and outperforms TMY at only 2 of the 27 sites.

The mechanism is a solar-resource-timing convexity. The reliability constraint makes cost a convex function of resource adversity: the worst sustained cloudy stretch sizes storage nonlinearly, and a TMY, assembled from independently selected typical months, tends to smooth over exactly the punishing multi-day stretches that drive the worst design years. This single convexity explains both the per-year right skew and TMY’s aggregate optimism.

A key consequence of this is that a system sized to a typical year may under-provision against a bad year and miss its uptime target. Site-specific, reliability-critical point designs should size against historical worst-stretch resource rather than a single representative year. Designing on a bootstrapped sample of historical years in sequence, or iteratively running the optimizer with the historical case year represent potential paths to address this.
